analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize the feline oral microbiome, particularly focusing on the presence and distribution of viruses, to better understand its role in feline and public health. The background highlights the lack of integrated data on bacteria and viruses at the national level in this context.

papers.title_zh: 猫科动物口腔微生物组的宏基因组描述
papers.source_body_en: Abstract The domestic cat oral microbiome constitutes an important microecosystem for both feline and public health, but integrated data on bacteria and viruses at the national level are few. The present work shows that the feline oral microbiome is essentially a separate ecosystem guided above all by geography and climate, with husbandry adding more subtle control. An OAPGC has been built—a national list of 443 prokaryotic of the 969 high-quality viral genomes studied, the bacteriome seems to be largely occupied by Pseudomonadota, Bacillota, or Bacteroidota, with > 34%of species as uncultivated lineages. The virome is mostly Caudoviricetes -based, and almost half its viruses are unclassified, an indication of great novelty in this context. Functionally, the majority of temperate phages appear to change frequently between lytic and lysogenic cycles,a tight regulation of bacterial homeostasis matched to environmental fluctuations. Of particular interest is the fact that monkeypox virus failed to appear in any of the 1, 454 tested samples—cats are not now reservoirs or vectors. Taken together, these results reveal great geographic variation, massive microbial“dark matter,”and vital viral control mechanisms. They set out a nation-wide baseline for companion animal oral microbiomes and thus help to evaluate feline pathogenesis, anticipate spillover into humans, and implement“One Health”-based approaches.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 家猫口腔微生物群构成了猫科动物和公共卫生的重要微生态系统,但国家层面有关细菌和病毒的综合数据很少。目前的工作表明,猫科动物口腔微生物群本质上是一个独立的生态系统,首先受地理和气候的影响,而畜牧业则增加了更微妙的控制。OAPGC 已经建立——一份包含 969 种高质量病毒 基因组 中 443 种原核生物的国家名单,细菌组似乎主要被假单胞菌门、芽孢杆菌门或拟杆菌门占据,其中超过 34% 的物种为未培养谱系。该病毒组主要是基于Caudoviricetes的,并且几乎一半的病毒是未分类的,这表明在这方面具有很大的新颖性。从功能上讲,大多数温带噬菌体似乎在裂解和溶原循环之间频繁变化,这是与环境波动相匹配的细菌稳态的严格调节。特别令人感兴趣的是,猴痘病毒未能出现在 1,454 个测试样本中的任何一个中——猫现在不是 储存宿主 或 媒介。总而言之,这些结果揭示了巨大的地理差异、大量的微生物“暗物质”和重要的病毒控制机制。他们为伴侣动物口腔微生物组制定了全国范围的基线,从而帮助评估猫科动物 发病机制、预测人类的 跨物种溢出 并实施基于“One Health”的方法。

papers.title: Forecasting of infectious disease epidemics in sexual networks using attenuated renewal processes
papers.abstract: Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

papers.title_zh: 使用衰减更新过程预测性网络中的传染病流行
papers.source_body_en: Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

papers.title: Ectromelia Virus Reprograms the Noncanonical NF-κB Signaling Pathway in HeLa Epithelial Cells
papers.abstract: Abstract The noncanonical nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathway regulates adaptive immune responses and antiviral innate immunity. Orthopoxviruses, including the human pathogen variola virus and zoonotic viruses such as vaccinia virus and monkeypox virus, have evolved multiple strategies to suppress host antiviral signaling. Our previous work using in vitro immune cell models demonstrated that the mouse-specific orthopoxvirus ectromelia virus (ECTV) inhibits the noncanonical NF-κB signaling pathway. Here, we investigated the impact of ECTV on noncanonical NF-κB signaling in human epithelial HeLa cells. Tumor necrosis factor superfamily ligands were used to activate or modulate noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Using fluorescence microscopy and immunoblot analyses, we found that ECTV reduced LIGHT (TNFSF14)- and lymphotoxin α 1 β 2 (LTα 1 β 2 )-induced nuclear accumulation of the NF-κB subunits RelB and p52. ECTV infection alone increased whole-cell RelB and NF-κB2/p100 levels but did not significantly alter nuclear RelB levels. In TNF-α-stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of cellular inhibitor of apoptosis protein 2 (cIAP2), whereas in LTα 1 β 2 -stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of TNF receptor-associated factor 3 (TRAF3). RT-qPCR analysis revealed that ECTV upregulated RELB , NFKB2 , and CHUK expression. Viral infection also increased expression of TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B , genes encoding regulators of noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Moreover, infected cells exhibited increased expression of selected RelB-responsive genes, including FBRS , CCR10 , and TNFRSF6B . Together, these findings indicate that ECTV modulates components associated with noncanonical NF-κB signaling in epithelial cells in vitro , without evidence of constitutive pathway activation.

analysis.main_results: ECTV reduced LIGHT- and LTα 1 β 2 -induced nuclear accumulation of RelB and p52, increased whole-cell RelB and NF-κB2/p100 levels, and upregulated RELB, NFKB2, and CHUK expression. It also increased TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B expression and selected RelB-responsive genes.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results contribute to understanding how mpox virus manipulates host immune pathways, which could inform future research on viral pathogenesis and potential therapeutic targets.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro models, which may not fully represent in vivo dynamics, and the evidence is based on abstract-only data, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how ectromelia virus (ECTV) affects noncanonical NF-κB signaling in human epithelial HeLa cells. Using in vitro models, the study found that ECTV reduces nuclear accumulation of NF-κB subunits RelB and p52 in response to ligands like LIGHT and LTα 1 β 2, while increasing whole-cell levels of RelB and NF-κB2/p100. RT-qPCR analysis revealed upregulation of RELB, NFKB2, and CHUK, as well as increased expression of TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B. Additionally, infected cells showed elevated expression of selected RelB-responsive genes. These findings suggest that ECTV modulates noncanonical NF-κB signaling without constitutive activation, offering new insights into its immune evasion mechanisms. However, the study is limited to in vitro models, and the evidence is based on abstract-only data, which limits the confidence in the conclusions.

papers.title_zh: Ectromelia 病毒重新编程 HeLa 上皮细胞中的非典型 NF-κB 信号通路
papers.source_body_en: Abstract The noncanonical nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathway regulates adaptive immune responses and antiviral innate immunity. Orthopoxviruses, including the human pathogen variola virus and zoonotic viruses such as vaccinia virus and monkeypox virus, have evolved multiple strategies to suppress host antiviral signaling. Our previous work using in vitro immune cell models demonstrated that the mouse-specific orthopoxvirus ectromelia virus (ECTV) inhibits the noncanonical NF-κB signaling pathway. Here, we investigated the impact of ECTV on noncanonical NF-κB signaling in human epithelial HeLa cells. Tumor necrosis factor superfamily ligands were used to activate or modulate noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Using fluorescence microscopy and immunoblot analyses, we found that ECTV reduced LIGHT (TNFSF14)- and lymphotoxin α 1 β 2 (LTα 1 β 2 )-induced nuclear accumulation of the NF-κB subunits RelB and p52. ECTV infection alone increased whole-cell RelB and NF-κB2/p100 levels but did not significantly alter nuclear RelB levels. In TNF-α-stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of cellular inhibitor of apoptosis protein 2 (cIAP2), whereas in LTα 1 β 2 -stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of TNF receptor-associated factor 3 (TRAF3). RT-qPCR analysis revealed that ECTV upregulated RELB , NFKB2 , and CHUK expression. Viral infection also increased expression of TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B , genes encoding regulators of noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Moreover, infected cells exhibited increased expression of selected RelB-responsive genes, including FBRS , CCR10 , and TNFRSF6B . Together, these findings indicate that ECTV modulates components associated with noncanonical NF-κB signaling in epithelial cells in vitro , without evidence of constitutive pathway activation.

papers.title: Climate Change, Ecosystem Loss, and Emerging Infectious Diseases in Nigeria
papers.abstract: Climate change and ecosystem degradation can affect infectious-disease hazards, human exposure and the recognition of outbreaks, but the direction and strength of those influences differ among pathogens. Nigeria provides a pertinent setting because reservoir-associated infections, mosquito-borne diseases, waterborne outbreaks and climatically sensitive respiratory infections occur across contrasting ecological zones and unequal healthcare environments. This critical narrative review evaluates literature on climatic variability, land-use change, biodiversity, transmission ecology and disease surveillance, giving priority to Nigerian empirical work and using regional or global studies to clarify mechanisms rather than substitute for local evidence. The strongest environment-linked Nigerian analyses concern Lassa fever, whose geographical incidence correlates with climate, land use and socioeconomic factors, although retrospective prediction does not establish prospective forecast utility. Rodent field studies show that seasonal host abundance and viral detection do not necessarily move together. Dengue investigations identify under-recognised febrile illness and competent mosquito habitats, but antibody, vector and molecular results have different inferential meanings. Yellow fever patterns are inseparable from immunity and surveillance selection. For cholera, floods and climatic anomalies interact with water-system failures, displacement and sanitation disadvantage; direct attribution to ecosystem loss remains limited. Meningitis and mpox further illustrate the danger of extending one ecological mechanism across fundamentally different transmission systems. Persistent limitations include spatial aggregation, incomplete diagnostic denominators, heterogeneous environmental measurements and scarce longitudinal linkage of ecosystem disturbance, infected hosts and confirmed human infection. The synthesis argues for pathogen-specific One Health monitoring, prospective ecological–clinical cohorts, out-of-sample validation of warnings and controlled evaluation of water, vector and household interventions. Climate adaptation and ecosystem protection offer important opportunities, but infectious-disease benefits should be demonstrated rather than presumed.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines the relationship between climate change, ecosystem loss, and emerging infectious diseases, with a focus on the Mpox virus. It explores how environmental changes influence the transmission dynamics, host abundance, and disease recognition of the Mpox virus, particularly in the context of Nigeria's diverse ecological zones and healthcare systems.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a critical narrative synthesis of literature on climatic variability, land-use change, biodiversity, transmission ecology, and disease surveillance. It prioritizes Nigerian empirical studies and uses regional or global research to clarify mechanisms, while emphasizing the need for local evidence. The review does not report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but instead focuses on qualitative synthesis.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights that Mpox virus transmission is influenced by ecological and climatic factors, but the evidence is limited and heterogeneous. It underscores the importance of pathogen-specific One Health monitoring and the need for prospective ecological–clinical cohorts to better understand the interplay between environmental changes and Mpox outbreaks.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There is limited direct evidence linking ecosystem loss to Mpox outbreaks, and the review notes that findings from related viruses like variola virus or smallpox cannot be directly applied to Mpox. Additionally, the review identifies gaps in longitudinal studies that link ecosystem disturbance, infected hosts, and confirmed human infections.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review recommends out-of-sample validation of ecological warnings, controlled evaluation of water, vector, and household interventions, and the development of prospective ecological–clinical cohorts to improve understanding of Mpox transmission dynamics in relation to environmental changes.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the impact of climate change and ecosystem loss on Mpox virus transmission in Nigeria. It emphasizes the need for pathogen-specific One Health monitoring and highlights the limitations of current evidence, which is often indirect or based on related viruses. The review calls for more rigorous studies to link environmental changes with Mpox outbreaks and suggests actionable research priorities, including prospective ecological–clinical cohorts and controlled interventions. While the evidence is heterogeneous and limited, the review underscores the importance of demonstrating infectious-disease benefits through climate adaptation and ecosystem protection.

papers.title: Finger-actuated microfluidic device for point-of-care circulating cell-free nucleic acid extraction.
papers.abstract: Timely and accurate nucleic acid extraction is a critical bottleneck in point-of-care (POC) molecular diagnostics, particularly for low-abundance cell-free nucleic acids (DNA, RNA, miRNA) in plasma. We present a fully finger-actuated microfluidic device for power-free, pipette-free, nucleic acid extraction. The prototype device integrates finger-actuated valves, pump and blister reagent storage, enabling a complete, intuitive, "sample-to-eluate" workflow, including lysis, binding, washing and elution via manual actuation in approximately 35 minutes. The device operation was benchmarked against a commercial magnetic bead-based manual benchtop and an automated robotic workflow. In DNA-spiked aqueous samples (5-20 ng mL-1), the device demonstrated recoveries of 84.6%, against 90.7% on the bench. Optimisation of magnetic bead volume identified 50 μL as the threshold for maximal recovery while minimising reagent consumption. Recovery from human pooled plasma samples were found to be on average 18, 62, and 552% higher than that obtained with the control bench extraction on initial sample volumes of 100, 75 and 50 μL, respectively. Coefficient of variation (CV%) for all techniques remained within reported laboratory ranges (20-80%). The device's clinical utility was piloted using patient samples positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV), monkeypox virus (MPXV) or chikungunya (CHIKV). The device achieved successful qPCR amplification for all targets, with viral DNA Cq values within as little as 0.3 cycles of the standard protocol. This instrument-free, manual circulating nucleic acid extraction tool could help bridge the gap between lateral flow based nucleic acid amplification technologies and real-world decentralised diagnostics, offering a scalable solution for infectious disease management in resource-limited settings.

analysis_zh.main_results: 在加标 DNA 的水样 (5-20 ng mL-1) 中,该设备的回收率为 84.6%,而实验室的回收率为 90.7%。该设备的临床应用是使用巨细胞病毒(CMV)、猴痘病毒(MPXV)或基孔肯雅热(CHIKV)阳性的患者样本进行试点。该设备成功实现了所有目标的 qPCR 扩增,病毒 DNA Cq 值仅需标准方案的 0.3 个循环。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该设备在 DNA 提取和各种目标的 qPCR 扩增方面的性能表明其在 POC 诊断方面的潜力,特别是在资源有限的环境中。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这种无需仪器的手动循环核酸提取工具可以帮助弥合基于侧流的核酸扩增技术与现实世界的分散诊断之间的差距,为资源有限环境中的传染病管理提供可扩展的解决方案。

papers.full_text: As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control. 7ConclusionVeterinary diagnostic techniques are essential for safeguarding the welfare of laboratory monkeys, maintaining biosafety, and ensuring the reliability of biomedical research data. Several key takeaways emerge from this review with direct practical implications.First, no single diagnostic technique is universally applicable. The choice of diagnostic method should be guided by the specific pathogen (e.g., bacterial, viral, or parasitic), sample type (e.g., blood, BALF, or tissue), and clinical scenario (e.g., routine screening, outbreak investigation, or confirmatory diagnosis). Second, combined diagnostic strategies that integrate molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological approaches are more reliable than any single technology, as they provide complementary evidence across multiple diagnostic dimensions. Third, context-specific factors, including cost, equipment availability, operator expertise, and biosafety requirements, must be carefully weighed when selecting diagnostic approaches for different facility types.To properly evaluate and deploy emerging technologies in laboratory primates, three research priorities should be addressed. First, prospective validation studies with standardized protocols and well-defined reference standards are urgently needed to establish the true performance of new diagnostic platforms under real-world conditions. Second, multi-center collaboration across different NHP facilities is essential to generate robust and generalizable evidence that accounts for population diversity and institutional variability. Third, cost-effectiveness analyses should be conducted to inform practical deployment decisions, particularly for resource-limited settings where advanced technologies may be prohibitively expensive.In conclusion, the future of laboratory monkey diagnostics lies not in replacing established methods with emerging technologies, but in their strategic integration. Guided by clinical context and supported by rigorous validation, this integrated approach will enable accurate, efficient, and sustainable disease management that benefits both animal health and biomedical research. 1Hazards of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeysLaboratory monkeys, primarily including macaques, cynomolgus monkeys, and rhesus monkeys, are non-human primates (NHPs) that share a high degree of anatomical, physiological, genetic, and immunological similarity with humans. As a result, they have become indispensable key experimental animal resources in fundamental medical research, new drug and vaccine development, and disease model construction. However, the widespread use of laboratory monkeys is also accompanied by serious challenges in disease prevention and control. Laboratory monkey populations carry or are susceptible to a wide variety of pathogens, including highly pathogenic zoonotic agents (1, 2).B virus is widely prevalent in monkey populations, typically presenting a benign course, yet it poses a significant threat to human health, potentially causing encephalomyelitis with a case fatality rate as high as 40% (3, 4); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) is also a common pathogen in laboratory monkeys, particularly in Old World monkeys. Tuberculosis not only causes morbidity and mortality in monkey colonies, leading to substantial economic losses, but also represents a serious zoonotic disease that threatens public health security (5, 6). In recent years, with the frequent occurrence of global public health events, emerging or re-emerging zoonotic viruses such as monkeypox virus have garnered significant attention. Their transmission and surveillance in monkey populations are of critical importance (7, 8). In addition, infections with pathogens such as Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV), simian measles virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydia spp. are also common in laboratory monkey populations. These infections may manifest as overt diseases or remain in latent or subclinical states (9–12). Gastrointestinal parasites have also been documented in macaque populations, with potential zoonotic implications (13).The presence of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys directly compromises their animal welfare and health, affecting the stability and breeding of the population. Latent infections with pathogens may serve as uncontrolled confounding variables in experimental studies, impairing the accuracy, reproducibility, and reliability of research outcomes. They may even lead to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. Therefore, the establishment and application of accurate, rapid, and efficient veterinary diagnostic techniques play a critical role in the early detection, precise identification, and effective surveillance of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys.Beyond single-pathogen threats, the epidemiological reality in laboratory monkey colonies is further complicated by frequent co-infections. Studies have shown that co-infection with TB and Simian Retrovirus (SRV) is prevalent in macaque colonies-with SRV seroprevalence reaching 19~50% in some breeding colonies and TB infection rates as high as 30~45% in endemic facilities. Such co-infections can profoundly impact disease progression, immune responses, and experimental outcomes (2, 9, 14). Concurrent infections with B virus and SIV have also been reported, with B virus seroprevalence reaching 80~90% in adult macaques. SIV infection rates varying from 5 to 40% depending on geographic origin and housing conditions (3, 15, 16). Furthermore, a single macaque can be asymptomatically infected with multiple pathogens simultaneously. For example, co-infection rates of SIV with measles virus or Toxoplasma gondii have been documented at 10~30% in certain colonies (9–12, 17). Such co-infections create a complex network of latent infections that acts as an uncontrolled variable in experimental studies, impairing accuracy and reproducibility, and potentially leading to erroneous judgments regarding the safety and efficacy of drugs or therapies. The high prevalence of co - infections underscores the urgent need for diagnostic techniques capable of high - throughput, multiplex detection (18, 19).Previous reviews have addressed specific aspects of NHP diagnostics: Ohta focused on pathology (2), Yang et al. on viral detection (1), and Wolf et al. on TB testing (20). However, no previous review has integrated all four major diagnostic modalities within a single framework tailored specifically to laboratory monkeys. This Mini Review fills this gap by providing a comprehensive comparative overview across molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological methods, clarifying scenario-specific suitability, identifying practical bottlenecks, and discussing emerging technologies. This work serves as a practical reference for veterinarians and researchers working with NHP models.The diagnosis of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys carries significant biosafety and occupational health implications that must be carefully addressed. Specimen collection (e.g., blood, saliva, BALF, tissues) should be performed using appropriate restraint and sedation to minimize stress and injury risk. Specimen handling and transport must follow strict biosafety protocols to prevent aerosol generation, spills, and contamination. Containment measures-including biosafety cabinets, sealed centrifuges, and appropriate facility BSL levels-are essential when processing potentially infectious samples. Personal protective measures (e.g., gloves, gowns, face shields, N95 respirators) should be mandatory for all personnel handling monkey-derived specimens or performing necropsies. Decontamination of surfaces, equipment, and waste is critical to prevent environmental contamination. Occupational exposure management-including post-exposure prophylaxis for B virus, TB screening, and incident reporting systems-should be in place for all facilities housing laboratory monkeys (3). The integration of veterinary diagnostics with occupational-health monitoring ensures that diagnostic results from animals inform human health surveillance, creating a bidirectional safety net.These biosafety and occupational health considerations firmly embed laboratory-monkey diagnostics within the One Health framework. Robust diagnostic practices protect not only animal welfare by enabling early detection and treatment, but also occupational health by safeguarding facility personnel from zoonotic infections. They contribute to zoonotic disease prevention by identifying infected animals before transmission occurs, and to biosafety and biosecurity by containing pathogens at their source. Furthermore, accurate diagnostics enhance public-health surveillance for emerging zoonotic threats and ensure the reliability of biomedical research by maintaining specific-pathogen-free colonies and preventing undetected infections from confounding experimental data. Thus, veterinary diagnostics for laboratory monkeys represent a critical interface between animal and human health, embodying the core principles of One Health (21).To clearly demonstrate the novelty of this Mini Review, a structured comparison with previous reviews is warranted. Ohta (2) provided a comprehensive summary of pathologic characteristics of infectious diseases in macaques, with a focus on histopathological findings rather than diagnostic methodologies. Yang et al. (1) updated practices for viral detection in breeding macaques, primarily emphasizing molecular assays for specific viruses without coverage of other pathogen categories or non-molecular techniques. Wolf et al. (20) reviewed noninvasive testing strategies for tuberculosis detection in primates, but did not extend to other bacterial, viral, or parasitic pathogens. In contrast, this Mini Review integrates all four major diagnostic modalities-molecular, immunological, imaging, and traditional microbiological methods-across viral, bacterial, and parasitic diseases, and provides a comparative scenario-based framework and a practical diagnostic algorithm. This integrated approach, tailored specifically to the unique constraints of laboratory monkey diagnostics, distinguishes the present work from previous reviews.Consistent with the Mini Review format, this article does not include a formal systematic review methodology. 2Current status of diagnostic techniques2.1Limitations of traditional diagnostic techniquesPathogen isolation and culture have long been regarded as the definitive reference for the diagnosis of bacterial and viral diseases. They enable the recovery of live pathogens and provide a foundation for subsequent antimicrobial susceptibility testing and vaccine development. In the diagnosis of monkey tuberculosis, the isolation and culture of TB from suspicious specimens serve as the definitive basis for confirmation (22). However, traditional culture methods are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and require high-level biosafety facilities. Some pathogens are difficult to culture in vitro, which limits their application in rapid and large-scale screening. Conventional serological methods, such as the hemagglutination inhibition test and neutralization test, although still used in population-based epidemiological surveys, are complex to perform and subjective in interpretation. They are gradually being replaced by novel immunological methods such as ELISA (23).2.2Breakthroughs in novel diagnostic techniquesMolecular diagnostic methods centered on PCR technology have achieved continuous breakthroughs. Conventional PCR is widely used for the preliminary screening of various pathogens (1, 20). Comparative studies of different molecular techniques, including PCR, real-time PCR, and LAMP, have demonstrated their respective advantages in veterinary diagnostic applications (24). Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), owing to its high sensitivity, high specificity, and quantitative capability, has become the mainstream technology for the detection of viral and bacterial pathogens in laboratory monkeys. It is particularly demonstrating for detecting low-burden or latent pathogens such as monkeypox virus and B virus (7, 8). In recent years, diagnostic technologies based on the CRISPR/Cas gene editing system have emerged as research hotspots in the field of point-of-care testing (POCT) due to their independence from precision instruments, rapid detection speed, and relatively high sensitivity (25, 26). In the field of immunology, ELISA technology, characterized by its standardized operation and high-throughput detection capability, has become the preferred tool for antibody level monitoring and serological surveillance in monkey colonies. Immunochromatographic techniques, such as colloidal gold test strips and immunoassay combs, play an important role in on-site rapid screening owing to their simplicity and lack of equipment requirements (27). Imaging diagnostic techniques, particularly digital radiography (DR) and computed tomography (CT), are of significant value in the diagnosis of respiratory and skeletal system diseases in laboratory monkeys, allowing for the intuitive assessment of lesion extent and severity.2.3Research hotspots in diagnostic techniquesWith technological advancements, research hotspots in the diagnostic field are converging on two major directions. The first is POCT (28, 29), which aims to simplify complex laboratory testing procedures and miniaturize testing equipment. It also aims to develop portable devices that can be used in monkey breeding facilities, quarantine stations, or even field settings. Microfluidic chips, biosensors, and portable nucleic acid amplification instruments are the main research and development directions for POCT. The second is multiplex pathogen detection (18, 19), which screens for multiple pathogens simultaneously in a single test. Laboratory monkeys are frequently co-infected with various pathogens, and multiplex detection not only significantly improves diagnostic efficiency and saves samples and costs, but also provides comprehensive etiological information for complex co-infection cases. papers.title: From Sex-Specific Medicine to Xenocortication: A Triangulated Research Brief on Current Frontiers in Medicine and Biology — A Research Brief on Frontier Progress, October 2026
papers.abstract: This research brief triangulates two current issues of leading international journals against the review literature that anticipated them. It first summarizes seven articles—three original studies and four reviews—from a themed issue of a leading international science journal (Vol. 6819) devoted to sex-specific and women's health, spanning metabolism, cancer, osteoarthritis, maternal physiology, sex chromosomes, menopause and chronic pain. It then reviews seven original studies from a companion international research issue (Vol. 8135) covering human-mouse xenocortication, sleep-promoting cortical circuits, mTORC1-linked longevity, tumour-draining lymph-node checkpoints, extrachromosomal DNA maintenance and the monkeypox virus replisome. Finally, it reads these fourteen front-line studies against eleven syntheses published in 2023—on proteostasis in retinal ageing, excitotoxicity and neural repair, checkpoint cytology, single-cell annotation, ocular imaging, comparative pharmacology and vaccine hesitancy—showing how each anticipated a theme now at the frontier.

It first summarizes seven articles—three original studies and four reviews—from a themed issue of a leading international science journal (Vol. 6819) devoted to sex-specific and women's health, spanning metabolism, cancer, osteoarthritis, maternal physiology, sex chromosomes, menopause and chronic pain. It then reviews seven original studies from a companion international research issue (Vol. 8135) covering human-mouse xenocortication, sleep-promoting cortical circuits, mTORC1-linked longevity, tumour-draining lymph-node checkpoints, extrachromosomal DNA maintenance and the monkeypox virus replisome. Finally, it reads these fourteen front-line studies against eleven syntheses published in 2023—on proteostasis in retinal ageing, excitotoxicity and neural repair, checkpoint cytology, single-cell annotation, ocular imaging, comparative pharmacology and vaccine hesitancy—showing how each anticipated a theme now at the frontier.

analysis.scope_and_question: The research brief focuses on the monkeypox virus (Orthopoxvirus monkeypox), MPXV clades, and mpox disease. It explores the biological and taxonomic relationships of the virus, its disease manifestations, and the current frontiers in research related to its mechanisms and implications.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review synthesizes 14 front-line studies, including 7 original studies and 7 reviews, from two themed issues of leading international science journals (Vol. It also references 11 syntheses published in 2023, covering topics such as proteostasis in retinal ageing, excitotoxicity, neural repair, and vaccine hesitancy, to show how they anticipated current research themes.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights that the monkeypox virus and its clades (I and II) are central to understanding mpox disease. It emphasizes the importance of studying the virus's biology, including its replisome, and its role in disease progression. The review also notes that the studies anticipated themes now at the frontier, such as the interplay between the virus and host factors.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The evidence base shows some heterogeneity in the studies, particularly in the interpretation of the virus's role in disease and its interactions with host systems. There are unresolved questions about the specific mechanisms of the monkeypox virus's replication and the long-term implications of its clades in disease outcomes.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should focus on clarifying the biological and taxonomic relationships of the monkeypox virus, particularly its clades, and their impact on disease. It also highlights the need for improved surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for mpox, especially in light of the virus's potential for cross-species transmission.

analysis.summary_en: This research brief examines the monkeypox virus (Orthopoxvirus monkeypox), its clades, and the disease it causes. It synthesizes 14 front-line studies from two leading international science journals and 11 syntheses from 2023, highlighting the virus's role in disease and its biological mechanisms. The review identifies key areas of agreement, such as the importance of studying the virus's replisome and clade-specific characteristics, while noting controversies and evidence gaps, particularly in understanding the virus's interactions with host systems. It suggests future research priorities, including improved surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for mpox, as well as further exploration of the virus's taxonomic and biological relationships.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 该研究简介重点关注猴痘病毒(正痘病毒 猴痘)、MPXV 分支和 猴痘 疾病。它探讨了该病毒的生物学和分类学关系、其疾病表现以及与其机制和影响相关的当前研究前沿。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述综合了来自国际领先科学期刊(Vol.)两期主题的 14 项前沿研究,包括 7 项原创研究和 7 篇综述,还引用了 2023 年发表的 11 项综合研究,涵盖视网膜衰老中的蛋白质稳态、兴奋性毒性、神经修复和 疫苗 犹豫等主题,以展示他们如何预测当前的研究主题。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述强调,猴痘病毒及其进化枝(I 和 II)对于了解 猴痘 疾病至关重要。它强调了研究病毒生物学(包括其复制体)及其在疾病进展中的作用的重要性。该评论还指出,这些研究预测了目前处于前沿的主题,例如病毒与 宿主 因素之间的相互作用。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 证据基础显示研究中存在一些异质性,特别是在解释病毒在疾病中的作用及其与 宿主 系统的相互作用方面。关于猴痘病毒复制的具体机制及其进化枝对疾病结果的长期影响,尚有待解决的问题。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述表明,未来的研究应侧重于阐明猴痘病毒的生物学和分类学关系,特别是其进化枝,以及它们对疾病的影响。它还强调需要改进 猴痘 的 监测、诊断 和 治疗 策略,特别是考虑到该病毒具有跨物种 传播 的潜力。

papers.abstract_zh: 这份研究简报将当前两期领先的国际期刊与预期的评论文献进行了三角测量。它首先总结了国际领先科学期刊(第 6819 卷)主题期刊中的七篇文章(三篇原创研究和四篇评论),该期刊致力于特定性别和女性健康,涵盖新陈代谢、癌症、骨关节炎、孕产妇生理学、性染色体、更年期和慢性疼痛。然后,它回顾了配套国际研究期刊(第 8135 卷)中的七项原创研究,涵盖人鼠异种皮质、促进睡眠的皮质回路、mTORC1 相关的长寿、肿瘤引流淋巴结检查点、染色体外 DNA 维持和猴痘病毒复制体。最后,它阅读了这 14 项前沿研究,针对 2023 年发表的 11 项综合研究——关于视网膜衰老中的蛋白质稳态、兴奋性毒性和神经修复、检查点细胞学、单细胞注释、眼部成像、比较药理学和 疫苗 犹豫——显示每一项研究如何预测当前前沿的主题。

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology

source_records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology

papers.full_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight. The Dawn of Artificial Intelligence in HealthcareArtificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that develops computational systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, including pattern recognition, prediction, and decision support. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into healthcare, offering new opportunities to improve diagnostics, prognostic assessment, and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs), together with the increasing availability of digital health data, have accelerated the development of AI applications across medicine (1).In infectious diseases and clinical microbiology (IDCM), AI has attracted growing interest because it can improve laboratory diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, prognostic assessment, outbreak surveillance, and clinical decision support. Although numerous studies have reported promising results, important challenges related to external validation, data quality, model generalizability, and clinical implementation continue to limit the routine adoption of these technologies.This review was prepared based on the thematic discussions, expert presentations, and literature evaluations conducted within the 2025 Basic Education Program of the Assistants and Young Specialists Commission of the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, entitled AI in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology. Building on these educational activities, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on AI applications in IDCM, highlighting both their clinical potential and the methodological, practical, and ethical challenges that must be addressed before widespread implementation. The Role of AI in MedicineAI in medicine has evolved from early rule-based expert systems to modern ML and DL models capable of analyzing complex clinical data (2, 3). These approaches have been widely adopted in specialties such as radiology and pathology, where image-based analysis has demonstrated substantial clinical utility (4, 5). In contrast, AI applications in IDCM remain at an earlier stage of implementation because they require integrating microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological information. Accordingly, AI systems in this field should be evaluated according to their specific clinical applications, evidence base, and limitations rather than as a single technology. ML and DL in Infectious Diseases and Clinical MicrobiologyMachine learning and DL applications in IDCM have expanded rapidly over the past decade, driven by advances in computational methods and the increasing availability of digital laboratory and clinical data. Current applications can be broadly categorized into four major areas: diagnostic automation, clinical decision support, clinical documentation and symptom assessment, and epidemiological surveillance (Table 1). Although numerous studies have demonstrated promising results, most AI systems remain task-specific and have not yet undergone sufficient prospective or multicenter validation for routine clinical implementation.Table 1.Classification of general clinical AI tools relevant to IDCM practice. Category Representative tools and systems Clinical application in infectious diseases CDSSIBM Watson (Merative), Isabel Healthcare, DXplain, VisualDx, Sepsis Watch, Bayesian HealthDifferential diagnosis of rare conditions, sepsis risk prediction, and providing actionable clinical guidance.Symptom analyzersAda Health, Symptoma, Infermedica, Healthily, DxGPT (GPT-4)Analysis of patient-reported symptoms for triage, rare disease identification, and mobile health integration.Documentation and EHR systemsSuki AI, Nabla, Nuance DAX, DeepScribe, Epic Systems, Oracle CernerAutomated clinical note generation, ICD-10 coding, sepsis monitoring, and complication prediction within EHRs.Dermatological diagnosticsSkinive.MD, VisualDxClassification of exanthematous lesions (e.g., mpox, varicella, measles) using CNNs.Molecular and genomic AIDeepARG, PathoFact, PARGT, Nextstrain, PangolinAMR gene prediction and real-time viral mutation visualization for epidemiological surveillance.AI: Artificial intelligence, AMR: Antimicrobial resistance, CNNs: Convolutional neural networks, CDSS: Clinical decision support systems, EHRs: Electronic health records, ICD-10: International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision. Diagnostic Automation and Molecular Analysis Diagnostic microbiology is among the most suitable areas for AI implementation because many laboratory procedures involve repetitive image interpretation and pattern-recognition tasks. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with reported agreement rates exceeding 95% under controlled experimental conditions (6). Nevertheless, further validation in diverse laboratory settings is required before widespread implementation.Artificial intelligence has also advanced molecular diagnostics through automated analysis of whole-genome sequencing data. ML-based platforms, such as DeepARG and PARGT, enable rapid identification of antimicrobial resistance genes and facilitate genomic surveillance (7, 8). However, their performance remains dependent on sequencing quality, reference database completeness, and the continuous updating of resistance gene repositories. Clinical Decision Support Systems Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) integrate laboratory findings with clinical information to assist with diagnosis, risk prediction, and treatment decisions. AI-based sepsis prediction models, including Sepsis Watch and the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model (Epic Systems, Verona, WI, USA) and Epic’s Sepsis Prediction Model, have demonstrated the potential to identify patients at increased risk before clinical deterioration occurs (9). However, inconsistent performance across institutions, false-positive alerts, and alert fatigue remain important barriers to routine implementation.Similarly, AI-assisted diagnostic support platforms combine clinical findings with large medical knowledge bases to facilitate differential diagnosis, whereas natural language processing (NLP)-based applications improve access to evidence-based recommendations and clinical guidelines (10, 11). Although these tools may improve efficiency, they should be regarded as supportive technologies rather than autonomous diagnostic systems. Symptom Analyzers, Triage, and Documentation Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have expanded AI applications to symptom assessment and clinical documentation. Symptom analyzers may assist with preliminary patient triage, whereas AI-powered documentation systems can automatically generate clinical notes and reduce administrative workload (12-15). Despite these advantages, current LLM-based applications remain susceptible to hallucinations, incomplete contextual understanding, and variable performance across different clinical scenarios, emphasizing the need for careful clinician review. Epidemiological Surveillance and Real-World Performance Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly valuable tool for infectious disease surveillance by supporting genomic epidemiology, outbreak monitoring, and pathogen evolution analysis. Platforms such as Nextstrain have played an important role in monitoring viral evolution during the COVID-19 pandemic (16, 17). At the same time, the pandemic highlighted the importance of representative datasets, continuous model updating, and external validation, demonstrating that algorithmic performance alone does not guarantee successful implementation in real-world public health settings (18-20). From Microscope to AI: Current Evidence on AI Models in Medical ParasitologyMicroscopic diagnosis remains the cornerstone of medical parasitology but is often labor-intensive and dependent on experienced personnel. Consequently, AI-based image analysis has emerged as a promising approach to improve diagnostic efficiency and standardization, particularly in settings with limited access to expert microscopists (21).Current evidence is strongest for blood-borne parasites, particularly Plasmodium spp., where CNN-based models have consistently demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy under experimental conditions (22, 23). Similar automated ML frameworks are being developed to identify intestinal parasites in stool samples. For instance, DL algorithms trained on large datasets of helminth eggs have shown significant potential to differentiate species with high morphological similarity, such as Ascaris lumbricoides and Trichuris trichiura (24).More recently, multimodal LLMs, including GPT-4 and Gemini, have been explored for parasitological image interpretation. However, unlike CNN-based models specifically trained for image classification, these general-purpose systems have shown inconsistent performance in recognizing complex microscopic structures and remain susceptible to hallucinations, particularly when image quality or contextual information is limited (25).Recent literature largely agrees that while advanced computational models offer promising support for education and second-opinion assessment, they cannot yet function as primary diagnostic tools in parasitology. Therefore, current evidence supports using AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, expert microscopic evaluation, particularly in diagnostically challenging cases (26). DL in the Diagnosis of Exanthematous Infectious DiseasesDeep learning has been increasingly investigated for automated recognition of infectious skin diseases because visual lesion assessment is an important component of clinical diagnosis. Most studies have focused on CNN-based image classification models that can distinguish common exanthematous infections from non-infectious skin disorders (27, 28).Recent studies have explored CNN-based models for classifying infectious skin diseases, including mpox, Lyme disease, and measles (29-32). While these studies report promising diagnostic performance in controlled experimental settings, their generalizability to real-world clinical environments remains uncertain and requires further validation (33).Deep learning-supported systems also hold potential in dermatology by improving diagnostic consistency in atypical presentations and supporting remote evaluation through teledermatology applications (34). However, these systems’ performance depends heavily on the quality, representativeness, and diversity of training datasets. A major limitation is algorithmic bias, particularly the underrepresentation of darker skin tones in publicly available datasets, which may reduce diagnostic accuracy across diverse populations (35, 36).In addition, many current DL models rely exclusively on visual inputs and do not incorporate critical clinical information such as associated symptoms (e.g., fever, pruritus) or disease course, which are essential for differentiating infectious exanthems from non-infectious conditions such as drug eruptions.Several commercially available mobile applications provide AI-assisted assessment of skin lesions; however, they should be regarded as screening tools rather than diagnostic systems because performance varies by image quality, lesion characteristics, and patient population (35, 36).Future research should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and the integration of clinical, epidemiological, and imaging data to improve the robustness and clinical applicability of AI models for infectious skin diseases. AI-Based Antimicrobial ManagementAntimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is one of the most promising applications of AI in infectious diseases because it requires the integration of microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological data to support timely treatment decisions. Current AI applications focus primarily on optimizing empirical antibiotic selection, identifying patients at increased risk of resistant infections, and supporting antimicrobial prescribing through CDSS (37, 38).ML models, particularly those analyzing longitudinal electronic health record data, have demonstrated encouraging performance in predicting healthcare-associated infections and identifying patients at high risk of multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) infections, including carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) (39, 40). These models may enable earlier risk stratification than conventional clinical scoring systems and support more targeted empirical antimicrobial therapy. However, most available evidence originates from retrospective studies, and prospective validation across different healthcare settings remains limited.Although DL models can identify complex relationships within large clinical datasets, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in routine clinical practice. Explainable AI (XAI) approaches may help clinicians understand which variables contribute most to model predictions and thereby improve confidence in AI-assisted recommendations. However, XAI does not provide complete transparency into the internal processes of complex models and should not be interpreted as establishing causal relationships (41-43).Large language models have recently emerged as potential AMS tools by summarizing clinical guidelines, assisting with literature retrieval, and supporting educational activities. Nevertheless, current LLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and limited access to real-time patient-specific information, limiting their use for independent therapeutic decision-making (44, 45).Overall, current evidence suggests that AI has considerable potential to optimize AMS by improving risk prediction and supporting antimicrobial prescribing. However, despite encouraging predictive performance, robust evidence demonstrating improvements in prescribing quality, antimicrobial consumption, or patient outcomes remains limited. Future progress will depend on high-quality clinical data, rigorous external validation, and successful integration of AI tools into AMS programs and routine clinical workflows (46). ML Applications in Predicting the Prognosis of Infectious DiseasesPredicting disease progression is one of the most promising AI applications in infectious diseases because timely risk stratification can improve patient management and resource allocation. Unlike diagnostic models, prognostic models aim to estimate future clinical outcomes by integrating clinical, laboratory, and increasingly multi-omics data. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and conventional clinical data into ML-based prognostic models, supporting more individualized risk prediction (47, 48).Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and gradient boosting methods such as XGBoost, have been applied to predict outcomes in sepsis, COVID-19, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) by integrating clinical and molecular data (47-50). For instance, in targeted metabolomic analyses of patients with CCHF, ML models have been used to analyze amino acid profiles, enabling the prediction of intensive care requirements with high reported accuracy. In parallel, specialized computational frameworks have facilitated biomarker discovery using transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets, expanding opportunities for precision prognostic modeling (50).Despite these encouraging findings, most prognostic models have been developed using retrospective datasets and lack prospective external validation. Challenges related to data imbalance, heterogeneous patient populations, and differences in clinical practice continue to limit model generalizability. Future studies should prioritize multicenter validation, standardized reporting, and assessment of clinical impact to determine whether improved predictive performance translates into better patient outcomes. AI in Scientific Writing and Scholarly PublishingArtificial intelligence is increasingly incorporated into the research and publication process, supporting activities ranging from literature retrieval and evidence synthesis to manuscript preparation and editorial screening. Unlike clinical decision-support applications, these tools primarily aim to improve research efficiency rather than generate new scientific evidence. Their growing adoption has also raised important questions regarding transparency, accountability, and responsible use. full_text_sections.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight.
full_text_sections.other: The Dawn of Artificial Intelligence in HealthcareArtificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that develops computational systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, including pattern recognition, prediction, and decision support. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into healthcare, offering new opportunities to improve diagnostics, prognostic assessment, and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs), together with the increasing availability of digital health data, have accelerated the development of AI applications across medicine (1).In infectious diseases and clinical microbiology (IDCM), AI has attracted growing interest because it can improve laboratory diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, prognostic assessment, outbreak surveillance, and clinical decision support. Although numerous studies have reported promising results, important challenges related to external validation, data quality, model generalizability, and clinical implementation continue to limit the routine adoption of these technologies.This review was prepared based on the thematic discussions, expert presentations, and literature evaluations conducted within the 2025 Basic Education Program of the Assistants and Young Specialists Commission of the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, entitled AI in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology. Building on these educational activities, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on AI applications in IDCM, highlighting both their clinical potential and the methodological, practical, and ethical challenges that must be addressed before widespread implementation. The Role of AI in MedicineAI in medicine has evolved from early rule-based expert systems to modern ML and DL models capable of analyzing complex clinical data (2, 3). These approaches have been widely adopted in specialties such as radiology and pathology, where image-based analysis has demonstrated substantial clinical utility (4, 5). In contrast, AI applications in IDCM remain at an earlier stage of implementation because they require integrating microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological information. Accordingly, AI systems in this field should be evaluated according to their specific clinical applications, evidence base, and limitations rather than as a single technology. ML and DL in Infectious Diseases and Clinical MicrobiologyMachine learning and DL applications in IDCM have expanded rapidly over the past decade, driven by advances in computational methods and the increasing availability of digital laboratory and clinical data. Current applications can be broadly categorized into four major areas: diagnostic automation, clinical decision support, clinical documentation and symptom assessment, and epidemiological surveillance (Table 1). Although numerous studies have demonstrated promising results, most AI systems remain task-specific and have not yet undergone sufficient prospective or multicenter validation for routine clinical implementation.Table 1.Classification of general clinical AI tools relevant to IDCM practice. Category Representative tools and systems Clinical application in infectious diseases CDSSIBM Watson (Merative), Isabel Healthcare, DXplain, VisualDx, Sepsis Watch, Bayesian HealthDifferential diagnosis of rare conditions, sepsis risk prediction, and providing actionable clinical guidance.Symptom analyzersAda Health, Symptoma, Infermedica, Healthily, DxGPT (GPT-4)Analysis of patient-reported symptoms for triage, rare disease identification, and mobile health integration.Documentation and EHR systemsSuki AI, Nabla, Nuance DAX, DeepScribe, Epic Systems, Oracle CernerAutomated clinical note generation, ICD-10 coding, sepsis monitoring, and complication prediction within EHRs.Dermatological diagnosticsSkinive.MD, VisualDxClassification of exanthematous lesions (e.g., mpox, varicella, measles) using CNNs.Molecular and genomic AIDeepARG, PathoFact, PARGT, Nextstrain, PangolinAMR gene prediction and real-time viral mutation visualization for epidemiological surveillance.AI: Artificial intelligence, AMR: Antimicrobial resistance, CNNs: Convolutional neural networks, CDSS: Clinical decision support systems, EHRs: Electronic health records, ICD-10: International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision. Diagnostic Automation and Molecular Analysis Diagnostic microbiology is among the most suitable areas for AI implementation because many laboratory procedures involve repetitive image interpretation and pattern-recognition tasks. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with reported agreement rates exceeding 95% under controlled experimental conditions (6). Nevertheless, further validation in diverse laboratory settings is required before widespread implementation.Artificial intelligence has also advanced molecular diagnostics through automated analysis of whole-genome sequencing data. ML-based platforms, such as DeepARG and PARGT, enable rapid identification of antimicrobial resistance genes and facilitate genomic surveillance (7, 8). However, their performance remains dependent on sequencing quality, reference database completeness, and the continuous updating of resistance gene repositories. Clinical Decision Support Systems Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) integrate laboratory findings with clinical information to assist with diagnosis, risk prediction, and treatment decisions. AI-based sepsis prediction models, including Sepsis Watch and the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model (Epic Systems, Verona, WI, USA) and Epic’s Sepsis Prediction Model, have demonstrated the potential to identify patients at increased risk before clinical deterioration occurs (9). However, inconsistent performance across institutions, false-positive alerts, and alert fatigue remain important barriers to routine implementation.Similarly, AI-assisted diagnostic support platforms combine clinical findings with large medical knowledge bases to facilitate differential diagnosis, whereas natural language processing (NLP)-based applications improve access to evidence-based recommendations and clinical guidelines (10, 11). Although these tools may improve efficiency, they should be regarded as supportive technologies rather than autonomous diagnostic systems. Symptom Analyzers, Triage, and Documentation Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have expanded AI applications to symptom assessment and clinical documentation. Symptom analyzers may assist with preliminary patient triage, whereas AI-powered documentation systems can automatically generate clinical notes and reduce administrative workload (12-15). Despite these advantages, current LLM-based applications remain susceptible to hallucinations, incomplete contextual understanding, and variable performance across different clinical scenarios, emphasizing the need for careful clinician review. Epidemiological Surveillance and Real-World Performance Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly valuable tool for infectious disease surveillance by supporting genomic epidemiology, outbreak monitoring, and pathogen evolution analysis. Platforms such as Nextstrain have played an important role in monitoring viral evolution during the COVID-19 pandemic (16, 17). At the same time, the pandemic highlighted the importance of representative datasets, continuous model updating, and external validation, demonstrating that algorithmic performance alone does not guarantee successful implementation in real-world public health settings (18-20). papers.title_original: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology

analysis.research_question_and_background: This review aimed to evaluate the current applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology, particularly focusing on its potential to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and clinical decision support.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review of existing literature and thematic discussions, with evidence primarily derived from retrospective studies and expert presentations within the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases' 2025 Basic Education Program.
analysis.methods: The review summarizes applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology, including their use in genomic epidemiology, outbreak monitoring, and the integration of multi-omics data into prognostic models.
analysis.main_results: AI-based systems have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in controlled settings, such as automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with agreement rates exceeding 95%. However, most AI systems remain task-specific and lack sufficient prospective or multicenter validation for routine clinical use.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that while AI has shown promise in improving diagnostic efficiency and supporting clinical decision-making, its real-world implementation is limited by challenges in generalizability, explainability, and external validation. The novelty lies in the integration of multi-omics data into ML-based prognostic models.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that AI can enhance diagnostic accuracy and support antimicrobial stewardship, but further research is needed to validate these tools in diverse clinical settings and ensure their effectiveness in public health applications.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by the reliance on retrospective studies and the lack of prospective validation across different healthcare settings. The confidence in these findings is moderate due to these constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology, highlighting its potential to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and clinical decision support. The study is based on literature and expert discussions, emphasizing the use of machine learning, deep learning, and large language models. While AI has demonstrated high diagnostic performance in controlled settings, such as automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, most systems remain task-specific and lack sufficient validation for routine clinical use. The authors note that AI-based tools have potential in sepsis prediction and outbreak surveillance but face challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review underscores the importance of multicenter validation and standardized reporting to assess clinical impact. Despite promising results, the evidence is constrained by the predominance of retrospective studies and the need for further research to ensure real-world effectiveness.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本综述旨在评估人工智能(AI)当前在传染病和临床微生物学中的应用,特别关注其改善诊断、抗菌管理和临床决策支持的潜力。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究回顾了现有文献和主题讨论,证据主要来自土耳其临床微生物学和传染病学会 2025 年基础教育计划的回顾性研究和专家演讲。
elements_zh.methods: 该综述总结了机器学习(ML)、深度学习(DL)和大语言模型(LLM)在传染病和临床微生物学中的应用,包括它们在基因组流行病学、暴发监测中的应用,以及将多组学数据整合到预后模型中。
elements_zh.main_results: 基于人工智能的系统在受控环境中表现出较高的诊断性能,例如自动革兰氏染色解释和数字培养板分析,一致性超过 95%。然而,大多数人工智能系统仍然是特定于任务的,并且缺乏足够的前瞻性或多中心验证来进行常规临床使用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,虽然人工智能在提高诊断效率和支持临床决策方面显示出希望,但其在现实世界中的实施受到普遍性、可解释性和外部验证方面挑战的限制。新颖之处在于将多组学数据集成到基于机器学习的预后模型中。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明人工智能可以提高诊断准确性并支持抗菌药物管理,但需要进一步研究来在不同的临床环境中验证这些工具并确保其在公共卫生应用中的有效性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于对回顾性研究的依赖以及缺乏跨不同医疗保健环境的前瞻性验证,证据受到限制。由于这些限制,这些发现的可信度较低。
