papers.full_text: The patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but needed chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was administered niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily life difficult, rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she developed ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform keratitis, leading to her presentation at our hospital. Examination of the right eye revealed disciform corneal edema and opacity, resulting in a diagnosis of disciform keratitis. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected via PCR analysis of the aqueous humor; treatment with oral valacyclovir and topical betamethasone was initiated. Subsequently, the disciform keratitis resolved with continued topical betamethasone therapy. However, ovarian cancer recurrence was observed, and another PARP inhibitor, olaparib, was prescribed. She again experienced malaise, necessitating the discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor. One month after discontinuation, a recurrence of disciform keratitis was observed. Frequent topical betamethasone administration was initiated, resulting in the resolution of the disciform keratitis. These findings suggest the possibility that in patients with cancer who are immunocompromised due to treatment with PARP inhibitors, an immune response against VZV does not occur; however, when immune function recovers upon discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor, the immune response against VZV is reactivated, resulting in the recurrence of disciform keratitis. Thus, when managing patients with cancer, it is essential to monitor fluctuations in immune response while addressing ocular infections and inflammatory diseases. DiscussionWhile herpetic keratitis is an ophthalmic disease, research in recent years has advanced beyond its purely ophthalmological aspects, such as diagnosis and treatment, to explore the relationship between the condition and systemic diseases. It has been reported that patients with diabetes face an increased risk of developing herpetic keratitis, as hyperglycemia can cause damage to the corneal epithelium [8]. In addition to the initial infection, the immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5]. Patients infected with the HIV, a prototypical immunodeficiency condition, are reported to experience a higher incidence of severe herpetic keratitis and a greater likelihood of recurrence [9-11]. Diabetes has been shown not only to cause corneal epithelial damage but also to impair immune responses systemically [12]. Consequently, a compromised immune response is considered a potential factor contributing to the development of herpetic keratitis in diabetic patients. These findings reinforce the understanding that the immune response is critical to the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5].There have been reports of patients developing herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated endotheliitis while receiving topical interferon (IFN)-α2b therapy for ocular surface squamous cell carcinoma [13]. Cases of disciform keratitis have also been reported in association with monkeypox virus (MPXV) infection, a condition frequently observed in immunocompromised individuals [14]. Although the condition initially resolved under the suspicion of herpetic keratitis, MPXV DNA was subsequently identified as the causative agent via PCR analysis of aqueous humor [14]. Thus, disciform keratitis can develop in various situations where immune suppression may occur. Furthermore, it is important to consider that pathogens not previously suspected of triggering disciform keratitis may also be potential causes of the condition.We encountered a case involving a patient with a history of ovarian cancer undergoing chemotherapy, in whom disciform keratitis developed, went into remission, and subsequently relapsed. The disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with a PARP inhibitor, a period characterized by systemic immunosuppression, but relapsed upon discontinuation of treatment. This pattern was observed repeatedly. As previously discussed, it is readily conceivable that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in the development of disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. However, there have been no reports in clinical practice that compare and analyze fluctuations in a patient's immune status alongside the clinical course of disciform keratitis. The information obtained from this case may provide evidence that systemic immune status contributes to the recurrence of disciform keratitis. However, data on hematological and immunological parameters (such as CBC with leukocyte differential and lymphocyte counts) were not available. Furthermore, this report demonstrated an association in a single case; it does not establish a causal relationship. The assertion that systemic immune status influences the resolution or recurrence of lesions lacks support from actual immunological data, and therefore, the hypothesis has not been empirically verified and has limitations.Taken altogether, for patients with cancer, it is essential, not only for disciform keratitis but also for determining treatment strategies for any ophthalmic condition, to verify and fully understand the details of their ongoing medical treatment and to correlate these with clinical ocular findings. ConclusionsIn a patient with a history of ovarian cancer, disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with PARP inhibitors. However, the condition was observed to recur following the discontinuation of chemotherapy. It has been reported that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. There have been no previous reports in clinical practice comparing and examining the relationship between changes in a patient's immune status and the course of disciform keratitis; thus, the information obtained from this case may provide valuable, direct evidence that systemic immune status influences the clinical course of disciform keratitis. IntroductionA condition in which the cornea becomes swollen in a disc-shaped pattern and cloudy is called disciform keratitis. Initially, disciform keratitis was known as "Arlt's abscessus siccus." In 1901, Fuchs renamed the condition "disciform keratitis" [1]. Disciform keratitis causes visual impairment due to corneal edema, opacity, and anterior chamber inflammation; furthermore, it can lead to a loss of corneal endothelial cells and result in bullous keratopathy [2]. Although the etiology of disciform keratitis was initially unclear, reports subsequently identified herpesviruses as a primary cause [3]. Regarding the pathogenesis, as the concept of immunology gained academic recognition, it was demonstrated that the condition involves not merely viral infection but also the host's biological response, specifically an immune response to viral antigens, which plays a crucial role [4]. It is now understood that the pathophysiology of disciform keratitis involves corneal stromal infiltration (predominantly by mononuclear leukocytes such as lymphocytes) and keratic precipitates, accompanied by disciform stromal edema and microcystic edema localized to the affected area [5]. Since these inflammatory cells infiltrate the eye locally via the systemic circulation, systemic immune status may significantly influence the onset of disciform keratitis. Recent reports indicate that, in addition to herpesviruses, other pathogens such as Acanthamoeba [6] and microsporidia [7] can also induce disciform keratitis.As noted above, while disciform keratitis may be triggered by an infectious process, the immune response plays a primary role in the development of the clinical presentation. While immunosuppression typically exacerbates rather than cures viral infections, it can serve to suppress inflammation in cases where the immune response to viral antigens triggers an inflammatory reaction. This report discusses a case in a patient with cancer in which the administration of anticancer drugs influenced the resolution and recurrence of disciform keratitis. Case presentationThe patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but continued chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was treated with the anticancer drug niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily activities difficult (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE): grade 3), rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor, which had been administered for five years, was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she noticed blurred vision with ocular pain and hyperemia. A few days later, she was diagnosed with ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform keratitis, leading her to visit our hospital. At the initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.2 in both eyes, and intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye. Disciform corneal edema and opacity, together with keratic precipitates and anterior chamber cells, were observed in the right eye (Figure 1), and a diagnosis of disciform keratitis was made.Figure 1Slit-lamp photographs at the initial visit.(a) Low magnification; (b) high magnification. Disciform keratitis is observed in the central cornea (dotted circle).Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected via PCR analysis of the aqueous humor; the patient was treated with oral valacyclovir for seven days and topical betamethasone, resulting in improvement.Table 1PCR results of aqueous humor samples.Type of pathogenPCR resultHerpes simplex virus type 1NegativeVaricella-zoster virusPositiveHerpes simplex virus type 2NegativeHuman herpesvirus 6NegativeEpstein-Barr virusNegativeCytomegalovirusNegativeHuman T-cell leukemia virus type 1NegativeTreponema pallidumNegativeToxoplasma gondiiNegativeSubsequently, the disciform keratitis resolved with continued topical betamethasone therapy (Figure 2).Figure 2Slit-lamp photograph two months after the initial visit.Disciform keratitis had resolved.Topical betamethasone therapy was completed six months after it began. Following a recurrence of ovarian cancer, the patient was prescribed olaparib, a PARP inhibitor. However, the patient again experienced physical deterioration (CTCAE: grade 3), leading to the discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor. One month after discontinuation, a recurrence of disciform keratitis was observed using the retroillumination method (Figure 3) because the lesion was mild.Figure 3Slit-lamp photograph one month after discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor olaparib.Retroillumination image. Recurrence of disciform keratitis is observed (dotted circle).PARP: Poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase.Consequently, frequent topical betamethasone administration was initiated; the disciform keratitis improved, and there has been no recurrence for three months (Figure 4).Figure 4Slit-lamp photograph two months after discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor olaparib.Retroillumination image. The disciform keratitis had resolved.PARP: Poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase.BCVA in both eyes remained around 1.2 during the observation period.

papers.title_original: Disciform Keratitis That Improves With Poly(Adenosine Diphosphate-Ribose) Polymerase Inhibitor Treatment for Ovarian Cancer but Recurs Upon Discontinuation of Treatment

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the relationship between immune status and the clinical course of disciform keratitis, particularly in the context of systemic immunosuppression caused by cancer treatments.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This case report describes a single patient with a history of ovarian cancer who developed disciform keratitis following discontinuation of PARP inhibitor therapy, highlighting the clinical course and immune status changes in this individual.
analysis.methods: Disciform keratitis was diagnosed via slit-lamp examination, and VZV DNA was detected using PCR analysis of aqueous humor. The patient was treated with oral valacyclovir and topical betamethasone, with clinical improvement observed.
analysis.main_results: Disciform keratitis resolved during PARP inhibitor treatment, which induced systemic immunosuppression, but recurred one year after discontinuation. PCR analysis confirmed the presence of VZV DNA in the aqueous humor.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that immune suppression from PARP inhibitors may prevent reactivation of VZV, leading to resolution of disciform keratitis, while immune recovery upon treatment discontinuation may reactivate the virus, causing recurrence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the importance of monitoring immune status in cancer patients to manage ocular complications like disciform keratitis, particularly those associated with viral reactivation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case, and the association observed does not establish causality. The evidence is considered moderate due to the lack of comparative data and immunological verification.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a patient with ovarian cancer who developed disciform keratitis following discontinuation of PARP inhibitor treatment. The condition resolved during treatment with the PARP inhibitor, which induced systemic immunosuppression, but recurred one year after treatment cessation. PCR analysis of aqueous humor confirmed the presence of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA, suggesting a link between immune status and the clinical course of disciform keratitis. The findings imply that immune suppression may prevent viral reactivation, while immune recovery could lead to recurrence. However, the study is limited to a single case and does not establish causality, resulting in moderate evidence strength. The report underscores the need to monitor immune status in cancer patients to manage ocular complications associated with viral reactivation.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the relationship between immune status and the clinical course of disciform keratitis, particularly in the context of systemic immunosuppression caused by cancer treatments.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: This case report describes a single patient with a history of ovarian cancer who developed disciform keratitis following discontinuation of PARP inhibitor therapy, highlighting the clinical course and immune status changes in this individual.
elements_en.methods: Disciform keratitis was diagnosed via slit-lamp examination, and VZV DNA was detected using PCR analysis of aqueous humor. The patient was treated with oral valacyclovir and topical betamethasone, with clinical improvement observed.
elements_en.main_results: Disciform keratitis resolved during PARP inhibitor treatment, which induced systemic immunosuppression, but recurred one year after discontinuation. PCR analysis confirmed the presence of VZV DNA in the aqueous humor.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that immune suppression from PARP inhibitors may prevent reactivation of VZV, leading to resolution of disciform keratitis, while immune recovery upon treatment discontinuation may reactivate the virus, causing recurrence.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the importance of monitoring immune status in cancer patients to manage ocular complications like disciform keratitis, particularly those associated with viral reactivation.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case, and the association observed does not establish causality. The evidence is considered moderate due to the lack of comparative data and immunological verification.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在探讨免疫状态与盘状角膜炎临床病程之间的关系,特别是在癌症 治疗 引起的全身免疫抑制的背景下。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本 病例报告 描述了一名有卵巢癌病史的患者,在停止 PARP 抑制剂治疗后出现盘状角膜炎,强调了该患者的临床病程和免疫状态变化。
elements_zh.methods: 通过裂隙灯检查诊断盘状角膜炎,并通过房水 PCR 分析检测 VZV DNA。该患者接受口服伐昔洛韦和局部倍他米松治疗,观察到临床改善。
elements_zh.main_results: PARP抑制剂治疗治疗期间盘状角膜炎得到缓解,该抑制剂诱导全身免疫抑制,但停药一年后复发。PCR 分析证实房水中存在 VZV DNA。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,PARP 抑制剂的免疫抑制可能会阻止 VZV 重新激活,从而解决盘状角膜炎,而 治疗 停药后的免疫恢复可能会重新激活病毒,导致复发。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该研究强调了监测癌症患者的免疫状态对于控制盘状角膜炎等眼部并发症的重要性,特别是与病毒再激活相关的并发症。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于单个案例,观察到的关联并不能确定因果关系。由于缺乏比较数据和免疫学验证,该证据被认为是中等的。

papers.source_body_en: These findings suggest the possibility that in patients with cancer who are immunocompromised due to treatment with PARP inhibitors, an immune response against VZV does not occur; however, when immune function recovers upon discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor, the immune response against VZV is reactivated, resulting in the recurrence of disciform keratitis. These findings reinforce the understanding that the immune response is critical to the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5].There have been reports of patients developing herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated endotheliitis while receiving topical interferon (IFN)-α2b therapy for ocular surface squamous cell carcinoma [13]. The assertion that systemic immune status influences the resolution or recurrence of lesions lacks support from actual immunological data, and therefore, the hypothesis has not been empirically verified and has limitations.Taken altogether, for patients with cancer, it is essential, not only for disciform keratitis but also for determining treatment strategies for any ophthalmic condition, to verify and fully understand the details of their ongoing medical treatment and to correlate these with clinical ocular findings. The patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but needed chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was administered niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily life difficult, rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she developed ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform ke...
papers.abstract_zh: 这些发现表明,在因使用PARP抑制剂而免疫功能受损的癌症患者中,针对水痘-带状疱疹病毒(VZV)的免疫应答可能不会发生;然而,当停止使用PARP抑制剂并恢复免疫功能时,针对VZV的免疫应答会被重新激活,导致盘状角膜炎的复发。这些发现加强了对免疫应答在疱疹性角膜炎发病机制中的关键作用的理解[5]。有报道称,接受局部干扰素(IFN)-α2b治疗以治疗角膜表面鳞状细胞癌的患者可能会出现单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)相关性内皮炎[13]。关于系统性免疫状态影响病变消退或复发的断言缺乏实际免疫学数据的支持,因此该假设尚未被实证验证且存在局限性。总体而言,对于癌症患者而言,不仅在盘状角膜炎的诊断中,而且在确定任何眼科疾病的治疗策略时,都必须核实并充分了解其正在进行的医学治疗,并将这些信息与临床眼科发现相关联。该患者为一名73岁女性。她接受了卵巢癌手术,但由于在切除边缘观察到肿瘤细胞,需要进行化疗。她接受了尼拉帕利二水合物(一种聚(腺苷二磷酸核糖)聚合酶(PARP)抑制剂)治疗五年;然而,她出现了严重的乏力症状,影响了日常生活,使得继续治疗变得不可能。因此,停止了PARP抑制剂的使用,其身体状况得到改善。停药一年后,她出现了眼部带状疱疹,随后发展为盘状角膜炎...

papers.title: Recomendaciones para el abordaje de infecciones de transmisión sexual en niños, niñas y adolescentes víctimas de violencia sexual
papers.abstract: La violencia sexual en niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA) constituye un grave problema de salud pública, con consecuencias físicas, psicológicas y sociales a corto y largo plazo. Dentro de sus complicaciones médicas, las infecciones de transmisión sexual (ITS) representan un desafío diagnóstico, terapéutico y médico-legal, particularmente en la población pediátrica. En Chile, las guías existentes han sido desarrolladas para la población adulta y no abordan de forma integral el manejo de ITS en NNA víctimas de violencia sexual (VVS). Este documento, elaborado por el Comité de VIH Pediátrico de la Sociedad Chilena de Pediatría, tiene como objetivo establecer recomendaciones actualizadas para el diagnóstico, profilaxis, tratamiento y seguimiento de ITS en NNA víctimas de violencia sexual, considerando la mejor evidencia científica disponible, realidad epidemiológica, normativa y farmacológica nacional. La metodología incluyó revisión crítica de literatura internacional y nacional, guías clínicas vigentes y consenso de expertos. Se abordan las principales ITS relevantes en este contexto –gonorrea, clamidiasis, tricomoniasis, sífilis, VIH/SIDA, hepatitis A, B y C, herpes simple, virus del papiloma humano y Mpox–, detallando indicaciones de toma de muestras, períodos ventana, esquemas terapéuticos, profilaxis post exposición, vacunación y seguimiento serológico. Estas recomendaciones buscan estandarizar el abordaje infectológico de NNA VVS en Chile, optimizando la pesquisa precoz, el tratamiento oportuno y las estrategias preventivas, en concordancia con la normativa nacional vigente.

analysis.summary_en: This study addresses the need for updated guidelines on the diagnosis, prevention, treatment, and follow-up of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in children, adolescents, and victims of sexual violence. The research question focuses on the challenges of managing STIs in this vulnerable population, particularly in the context of sexual violence. The study design is based on a critical review of existing literature, clinical guidelines, and expert consensus. The methods involved analyzing the most relevant STIs, including mpox, and detailing sampling protocols, window periods, therapeutic schemes, post-exposure prophylaxis, vaccination, and serological follow-up. The main results include the establishment of comprehensive recommendations for the management of STIs in children and adolescents affected by sexual violence. The authors interpret these findings as a means to standardize the infectious approach in this population, aligning with national regulations. The scientific and public health significance lies in the potential to improve early detection, timely treatment, and preventive strategies in Chile. However, the evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on literature review and expert consensus rather than original studies or statistical data.

papers.title_zh: 关于儿童、儿童和青少年性暴力受害者的性传播感染的建议
papers.source_body_en: La violencia sexual en niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA) constituye un grave problema de salud pública, con consecuencias físicas, psicológicas y sociales a corto y largo plazo. Dentro de sus complicaciones médicas, las infecciones de transmisión sexual (ITS) representan un desafío diagnóstico, terapéutico y médico-legal, particularmente en la población pediátrica. En Chile, las guías existentes han sido desarrolladas para la población adulta y no abordan de forma integral el manejo de ITS en NNA víctimas de violencia sexual (VVS). Este documento, elaborado por el Comité de VIH Pediátrico de la Sociedad Chilena de Pediatría, tiene como objetivo establecer recomendaciones actualizadas para el diagnóstico, profilaxis, tratamiento y seguimiento de ITS en NNA víctimas de violencia sexual, considerando la mejor evidencia científica disponible, realidad epidemiológica, normativa y farmacológica nacional. La metodología incluyó revisión crítica de literatura internacional y nacional, guías clínicas vigentes y consenso de expertos. Se abordan las principales ITS relevantes en este contexto –gonorrea, clamidiasis, tricomoniasis, sífilis, VIH/SIDA, hepatitis A, B y C, herpes simple, virus del papiloma humano y Mpox–, detallando indicaciones de toma de muestras, períodos ventana, esquemas terapéuticos, profilaxis post exposición, vacunación y seguimiento serológico. Estas recomendaciones buscan estandarizar el abordaje infectológico de NNA VVS en Chile, optimizando la pesquisa precoz, el tratamiento oportuno y las estrategias preventivas, en concordancia con la normativa nacional vigente.
papers.abstract_zh: 儿童、儿童和青少年的性暴力(NNA)构成了公共健康、暴力、精神和社会问题的严重问题。医疗并发症、性传播感染 (ITS) 代表了诊断、治疗和医疗法律、特别是儿科疾病的解决方案。在智利,存在成人暴力的问题,并且没有放弃 ITS 和 NNA 性暴力受害者 (VVS) 的完整规定。该文件由智利儿科协会 VIH 儿科委员会详细阐述,旨在为诊断、剖析、ITS 和 NNA 性暴力受害者的实际建议提供客观建议,并考虑最佳证据科学、现实的流行病学、规范和国家农业科学。方法论包括对国际和国内文学批评的修订、临床指导和专家共识。Se abordan las primes ITS relatedes en este contexto –淋病、衣原体病、滴虫病、sífilis、VIH/SIDA、甲型、B型和C型肝炎、单纯疱疹、人类乳头瘤病毒和猴痘–、detallando indicaciones de toma de muestras、períodos ventana、esquemas terapéuticos、profilaxis post展览、真空和血清学研究。建议智利 NNA VVS 采取预防感染措施,优化预防措施、机会和预防策略,并与国家规范保持一致。

papers.full_text: 586 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 Harnessing the true potential of artificial intelligence for health emergency preparedness and response in complex settings Muhammad Tariq1, Zubrain Aamer Ikram2, Mona Elbarbary3 and Thomas Mollet3 1School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering, National University of Sciences and Technology Islamabad, Pakistan (Correspondence to Muhammad Tariq: muhammad.tariq@smme.nust.edu.pk). 2Development Synergies International, Islamabad, Pakistan. 3World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, Cairo, Egypt. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI, health emergency, preparedness and response, conflict-affected, Eastern Mediterranean Citation: Tariq M, Ikram ZA, Elbarbary M, Mollet T. Harnessing the true potential of artificial intelligence for health emergency preparedness and response in complex settings. East Mediterr Health J. 2026;32(9):586–588. https://doi.org/10.26719/2026.32.9.586. Received: 22/06/2026; Accepted: 01/09/2026 Copyright © Authors 2026; Licensee: World Health Organization. EMHJ is an open-access journal. This paper is available under the Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial ShareAlike 3.0 IGO licence (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/igo). The Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) continues to bear a disproportionate share of the world’s health emergencies. As of 2025, WHO was actively responding to 16 concurrent emergencies in the region, with more than 115 million people requiring urgent humanitarian assistance and two-thirds of all global attacks on health care facilities occurring within its borders (1,2). Protracted conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Yemen continue to devastate health infrastructure, while recurring infectious disease threats including cholera, poliovirus re-emergence and Mpox further strain overwhelmed health systems. In January 2025, WHO appealed for US $ 856 million to sustain emergency health operations across Member States (3). The scale and complexity of these overlapping crises indicate the need to complement conventional public health tools with innovative approaches. Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding at an unprecedented pace across almost every domain of human activity, including health. Machine learning, natural language processing and large-scale data analytics are now enabling health systems to process volumes and varieties of information that would simply not be feasible manually (4). The COVID-19 pandemic marked a pivotal inflection point, demonstrating the capacity of AI to accelerate genome sequencing, support vaccine development and monitor disease spread in near real-time across multiple countries simultaneously (5). Globally, AI is now embedded in diagnostic imaging, clinical decision support, genomic surveillance, drug discovery, and population health analytics, and its integration into public health practice continues to accelerate. In the specific context of health emergencies such as those faced in several EMR countries, AI offers powerful capabilities for disease surveillance, early outbreak detection and human ability to respond applying innovative detection approaches. Setting a performance standard of detection, investigation, notification, and initiation of response allows for the assessment of the performance of surveillance, reporting, investigation, and response systems. Platforms such as EPIWATCH and WHO’s Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) system continuously scan thousands of data streams, including news reports, social media, electronic health records, and travel data, detecting disease emergence signals often days or weeks before official notifications are issued (6,7). Natural language processing tools capable of handling multilingual data are particularly relevant to the EMR, where health information is generated in the predominant languages of Arabic, English, French, and other languages, and where social media may serve as an early warning indicator in conflict-affected settings with limited formal reporting infrastructure (8). Machine learning models have demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for specific outbreak risks, including cholera outbreak prediction models achieving up to 99.62 % accuracy in resource-constrained settings while similar AI frameworks have been deployed by entities like UNICEF and others to pre-empt disease resurgence (9). Beyond surveillance, AI holds considerable promise for operational preparedness and emergency response. Predictive analytics can support scenario planning and risk stratification, enabling health authorities to anticipate outbreak trajectories and pre-position medical supplies accordingly (10). In settings where supply chains are routinely disrupted by conflict and population displacement, a persistent challenge across the EMR countries, AI tools can optimise the real-time allocation of vaccines, diagnostics and health personnel to where they are needed most (11). Automated contact-tracing algorithms can rapidly map exposure networks and interrupt transmission chains, significantly reducing the burden on human health workers already stretched to capacity (12). AI-based risk modeling can further assist policymakers in resource-constrained settings to prioritise preventive interventions and build the case for sustained investment in preparedness, potentially averting far greater costs downstream. The WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean has taken meaningful steps to translate this potential into action. In April 2026, it launched a Community of Practice on AI for Disaster and Emergency Response Surveillance, bringing together national health authorities, researchers and partners to co-develop practical guidance for applying AI safely, ethically and effectively in regional surveillance and response 587 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 operations (13). This followed the May 2025 launch of the All-Hazards Information Management (AIM) toolkit, an AI-powered platform designed to improve the speed, clarity and consistency of emergency information management across Member States (14). A regional AI literacy workshop held in Amman in December 2025 further sought to build institutional capacity for evaluating, governing and scaling AI solutions within national health systems (15). Despite this momentum, real challenges remain: the AI literacy, data quality and interoperability gaps, limited digital infrastructure in fragile and conflict-affected states, concerns around algorithmic bias and data privacy, and the risk of AI deepening existing inequities between better- and lesser-resourced health systems must be addressed with equal seriousness. The convergence of escalating health emergencies and rapidly maturing AI technologies presents health systems in the EMR with a timely and important opportunity. AI-enabled surveillance can reduce outbreak detection time from weeks to days, translating directly into lives saved and costs averted with estimates suggesting that earlier detection and faster response can reduce epidemic response expenditure by up to 40 %, with corresponding improvements in mortality outcomes (16). To fully realise these benefits, the region must invest in harmonised data systems, cross-border information sharing frameworks, and governance structures that ensure AI is deployed equitably and with appropriate human oversight. Translating this opportunity into measurable gain requires action on 4 fronts. First, ministries of health should position AI within existing national health emergency preparedness structures, including national action plans for health security and International Health Regulations (2005) core capacity strengthening, rather than as freestanding pilot projects that rarely outlive their funding cycles. Second, investment should be sequenced so that data foundations precede algorithms: interoperability standards, case-based reporting and routine data quality assurance determine the standards of any model performance, and AI deployed on fragmented data will reproduce that fragmentation at speed despite using any reinforcement modelling. Third, regional governance should be made explicit, through minimum standards for model validation, data protection and human oversight, anchored in the 6 consensus principles set out in WHO guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health (17). Fourth, AI literacy should be embedded in the curricula of the field epidemiology training programmes and in the standard operating procedures of national and subnational emergency operations centres, so that epidemiologists are equipped to interrogate, verify and, where necessary, override machine-generated signals rather than simply receive them. Across all these 4 fronts, deployment in fragile and conflict-affected states requires early priority and design for low bandwidth, intermittent connectivity conditions; if AI is scaled first where infrastructure is already strong, it risks widening the inequities AI is being introduced to reduce. These gaps define a concrete research agenda for the EMR. Prospective evaluations are needed of AI-enabled event-based surveillance in EMR settings, reporting not only gains in detection timeliness but false-signal burden and the human verification workload generated, benchmarked against established standards for detection, notification and initiation of response. Predictive models developed elsewhere, including the cholera forecasting models earlier noted, require external validation on regional datasets before their reported accuracy can be assumed to transfer to EMR or global epidemiologic and data environments. Implementation research is needed on what is operationally feasible in conflict-affected settings characterised by damaged infrastructure, displaced populations and interrupted data flows, where constraints differ fundamentally from those of the settings in which most tools are developed. Economic evaluations should test whether projected savings from earlier detection hold under regional cost structures and health system configurations. Algorithmic performance requires examination specifically for displaced, undocumented and linguistic minority populations, who are systematically under- represented in training data yet bear a disproportionate share of the burden of health emergencies in the EMR. The promise of AI in health emergencies extends beyond technology and the power of using the existing AI tools and instruments. It is ultimately about building more resilient health systems capable of protecting people when it matters most, at a time when the region can least afford to be unprepared. Funding: None. The Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) continues to bear a disproportionate share of the world’s health emergencies. As of 2025, WHO was actively responding to 16 concurrent emergencies in the region, with more than 115 million people requiring urgent humanitarian assistance and two-thirds of all global attacks on health care facilities occurring within its borders (1,2). Protracted conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Yemen continue to devastate health infrastructure, while recurring infectious disease threats including cholera, poliovirus re-emergence and Mpox further strain overwhelmed health systems. In January 2025, WHO appealed for US $ 856 million to sustain emergency health operations across Member States (3). The scale and complexity of these overlapping crises indicate the need to complement conventional public health tools with innovative approaches. Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding at an unprecedented pace across almost every domain of human activity, including health. Machine learning, natural language processing and large-scale data analytics are now enabling health systems to process volumes and varieties of information that would simply not be feasible manually (4). The COVID-19 pandemic marked a pivotal inflection point, demonstrating the capacity of AI to accelerate genome sequencing, support vaccine development and monitor disease spread in near real-time across multiple countries simultaneously (5). Globally, AI is now embedded in diagnostic imaging, clinical decision support, genomic surveillance, drug discovery, and population health analytics, and its integration into public health practice continues to accelerate. In the specific context of health emergencies such as those faced in several EMR countries, AI offers powerful capabilities for disease surveillance, early outbreak detection and human ability to respond applying innovative detection approaches. Setting a performance standard of detection, investigation, notification, and initiation of response allows for the assessment of the performance of surveillance, reporting, investigation, and response systems. Platforms such as EPIWATCH and WHO’s Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) system continuously scan thousands of data streams, including news reports, social media, electronic health records, and travel data, detecting disease emergence signals often days or weeks before official notifications are issued (6,7). Natural language processing tools capable of handling multilingual data are particularly relevant to the EMR, where health information is generated in the predominant languages of Arabic, English, French, and other languages, and where social media may serve as an early warning indicator in conflict-affected settings with limited formal reporting infrastructure (8). Machine learning models have demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for specific outbreak risks, including cholera outbreak prediction models achieving up to 99.62 % accuracy in resource-constrained settings while similar AI frameworks have been deployed by entities like UNICEF and others to pre-empt disease resurgence (9). Beyond surveillance, AI holds considerable promise for operational preparedness and emergency response. Predictive analytics can support scenario planning and risk stratification, enabling health authorities to anticipate outbreak trajectories and pre-position medical supplies accordingly (10). In settings where supply chains are routinely disrupted by conflict and population displacement, a persistent challenge across the EMR countries, AI tools can optimise the real-time allocation of vaccines, diagnostics and health personnel to where they are needed most (11). Automated contact-tracing algorithms can rapidly map exposure networks and interrupt transmission chains, significantly reducing the burden on human health workers already stretched to capacity (12). AI-based risk modeling can further assist policymakers in resource-constrained settings to prioritise preventive interventions and build the case for sustained investment in preparedness, potentially averting far greater costs downstream. The WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean has taken meaningful steps to translate this potential into action. In April 2026, it launched a Community of Practice on AI for Disaster and Emergency Response Surveillance, bringing together national health authorities, researchers and partners to co-develop practical guidance for applying AI safely, ethically and effectively in regional surveillance and response 587 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 operations (13). This followed the May 2025 launch of the All-Hazards Information Management (AIM) toolkit, an AI-powered platform designed to improve the speed, clarity and consistency of emergency information management across Member States (14). A regional AI literacy workshop held in Amman in December 2025 further sought to build institutional capacity for evaluating, governing and scaling AI solutions within national health systems (15). Despite this momentum, real challenges remain: the AI literacy, data quality and interoperability gaps, limited digital infrastructure in fragile and conflict-affected states, concerns around algorithmic bias and data privacy, and the risk of AI deepening existing inequities between better- and lesser-resourced health systems must be addressed with equal seriousness. The convergence of escalating health emergencies and rapidly maturing AI technologies presents health systems in the EMR with a timely and important opportunity. AI-enabled surveillance can reduce outbreak detection time from weeks to days, translating directly into lives saved and costs averted with estimates suggesting that earlier detection and faster response can reduce epidemic response expenditure by up to 40 %, with corresponding improvements in mortality outcomes (16). To fully realise these benefits, the region must invest in harmonised data systems, cross-border information sharing frameworks, and governance structures that ensure AI is deployed equitably and with appropriate human oversight. Translating this opportunity into measurable gain requires action on 4 fronts. First, ministries of health should position AI within existing national health emergency preparedness structures, including national action plans for health security and International Health Regulations (2005) core capacity strengthening, rather than as freestanding pilot projects that rarely outlive their funding cycles. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance health emergency preparedness and response, particularly in complex settings like the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR), where health emergencies are frequent and resource constraints are significant.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on the EMR, where as of 2025, WHO was responding to 16 concurrent health emergencies affecting over 115 million people. It examined the application of AI in health emergency contexts, including surveillance, outbreak detection, and response strategies.
analysis.methods: The study discussed the use of machine learning, natural language processing, and large-scale data analytics to process health-related information. It highlighted AI's role in accelerating genome sequencing, supporting vaccine development, and monitoring disease spread in real-time across multiple countries.
analysis.main_results: The study found that predictive models for cholera outbreaks achieved up to 99.62% accuracy in resource-constrained settings. However, it emphasized that these models require external validation on regional datasets before their accuracy can be assumed to apply to the EMR or global environments.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that AI-based risk modeling can help prioritize preventive interventions and justify investment in preparedness, which could lead to significant cost savings and improved health outcomes. This approach is novel in its focus on integrating AI into public health systems for emergency response.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that AI can be a valuable tool for improving disease surveillance and response in the EMR, where health emergencies are frequent and complex. This could lead to more efficient allocation of resources and better preparedness for future outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study notes that predictive models developed elsewhere require external validation on regional datasets, which limits their immediate applicability. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on existing AI applications and highlights the need for further testing in EMR-specific contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance health emergency preparedness and response in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR), where health emergencies are frequent and complex. It highlights the use of AI in disease surveillance, outbreak prediction, and real-time monitoring, emphasizing the need for external validation of predictive models in EMR settings. The authors suggest that AI can support resource allocation and justify investment in preparedness, potentially reducing costs and improving health outcomes. However, the study notes that AI applications must be adapted to local data environments and that current models require further testing to ensure their effectiveness in the EMR. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on existing AI applications and underscores the importance of data quality and regional validation for successful implementation.

analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,人工智能可以成为改善疾病 监测 和电子病历 (EMR) 响应的宝贵工具,因为电子病历中的突发卫生事件频繁且复杂。这可能会导致更有效的资源分配,并为未来的 暴发 做好更好的准备。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究指出,其他地方开发的预测模型需要对区域数据集进行外部验证,这限制了它们的直接适用性。证据是温和的,因为它依赖于现有的人工智能应用程序,并强调需要在特定于电子病历的环境中进行进一步测试。

What to know There are two types of the virus that causes monkeypox, clade I and clade II. Both types can be spread, treated, and prevented in the same ways. Each clade has two subclades (clade Ia and clade Ib; clade IIa and IIb). Recent outbreaks of monkeypox have spread initially through intimate or sexual contact. In some cases, monkeypox was then spread within households. Recent travel-associated clade I monkeypox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib; there have been no deaths associated with these cases and most people had relatively mild illness. The ongoing global outbreak of clade IIb monkeypox that began in 2022 has caused more than 100,000 cases in more than 120 total countries. CDC has vaccination recommendations for people at risk in the United States or who are traveling to countries with clade I outbreaks or new clade II outbreaks. Current situation In the United States Clade I monkeypox The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low. In the United States, since November 2024, there have been more than 90 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox in at least 23 states plus Puerto Rico. The majority of these cases are among gay, bisexual, or other men who have sex with men. Many of these cases: Had recently traveled from areas associated with the outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa; Reported sexual contact during travel to parts of Western Europe where newer outbreaks are being reported; OR Reported sexual contact with people who had traveled from these areas. Since August 2026, an increasing proportion of clade I cases in the United States have been reported in individuals with no recent international travel or known links to people who had recently traveled. Cases with presumed domestic transmission have been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions, indicating a likely transition to sustained clade Ib transmission in the United States CDC expects to see additional cases of both travel-related and domestically acquired cases of clade Ib occurring across the United States. CDC continues to monitor both clade II and clade I monkeypox cases across the United States and follow surveillance reports to monitor for any changes in demographics, disease severity, or case counts by jurisdiction. CDC also continues surveillance testing to identify monkeypox clade for all specimens sent to CDC's poxvirus laboratory. Spotlight Jurisdictions can contact poxvirus@cdc.gov for CDC technical support and clinical consultations for severe cases Monday-Friday, 8 a.m.-5 p.m. Clade II monkeypox Clade II monkeypox is still circulating at low levels. Fall 2025 marked the highest monthly case counts since the peak of the outbreak in 2022. Reminder Vaccination is an important tool in stopping the spread of monkeypox. If you have certain risk factors that make you eligible, you can help protect yourself from monkeypox by getting the 2-dose monkeypox vaccine. Monkeypox Vaccination Across the globe Clade I monkeypox Outbreaks of clade I monkeypox in Central and Eastern Africa continue. Beginning in Fall 2025, several countries in Western Europe began reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to male-to-male sexual contact. Other travel-associated cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported from other parts of Africa, as well as Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North America, South America, and Australia. Recent monkeypox outbreaks have low death rates During recent outbreaks, death rates ranged from than less than 0.5% (clade Ib) to about 3% (clade Ia). Clade II is the type that caused the ongoing global outbreak that began in 2022. Fewer than 0.1% of people infected with clade II die from the disease. Clade II monkeypox For global case data for clade I and clade II monkeypox since January 1, 2024, see Global Mpox Trends. Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. Clade I Monkeypox Outbreaks Cases of clade I monkeypox have been diagnosed worldwide. Clade II Monkeypox Outbreaks Clade II monkeypox is spreading in the United States and around the world. What CDC is doing CDC raises awareness for U.S. healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC continues critical work to protect the United States from emerging and infectious diseases. CDC has collaborated closely with key partners in affected countries to help support efforts to stop monkeypox at the source. CDC works closely with U.S. state, tribal, local, and territorial public health departments to provide recommendations for clinical management, diagnosis, and prevention of domestic monkeypox cases. in the U.S. CDC continually increases capacity in communities across the United States for early detection of monkeypox through existing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing. CDC raises awareness for healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC collaborated with governmental and civil society partners in affected countries to collect and analyze case data, and to identify how monkeypox is spreading. CDC coordinated technical assistance in response to urgent in-country needs, including: increasing the number of monkeypox testing sites; improving specimen transport networks to quickly identify new cases; assisting with Ministry of Health-led vaccine implementation; strengthening emergency management systems; improving case surveillance; and training healthcare workers. CDC's staff throughout Africa provide critical, real-time information to inform U.S. preparedness efforts. In the United States CDC works closely with state, tribal, local, and territorial public health departments to provide recommendations for clinical management, diagnosis, and prevention of monkeypox cases in the U.S. CDC continually increases capacity in communities across the United States for early detection of monkeypox through existing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing. CDC raises awareness for healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC has information and recommendations for members of the public, including travelers: Destinations | Travelers' Health, Travel Health Notices, and Health Alert Network advisories. CDC continues to work with international partners to help reduce monkeypox transmission. analysis.time: monkeypox outbreak has been ongoing since November 2024, with recent cases reported as of August 2026. The global outbreak began in 2022, and the highest monthly case counts since then were observed in Fall 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: The United States and over 120 countries globally. In the U.S., cases have been reported in at least 23 states plus Puerto Rico, with a majority among gay, bisexual, or other men who have sex with men.
analysis.event: Monkeypox outbreaks, including both clade I and clade II, are ongoing. Recent outbreaks have primarily spread through intimate or sexual contact, with some cases involving household transmission. The CDC reports that clade I outbreaks have been attributed to subclade Ib, and clade II outbreaks have been ongoing since 2022.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The ongoing global outbreak of clade II monkeypox has caused more than 100,000 cases in over 120 countries. In the U.S., since November 2024, there have been more than 90 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox. The risk posed by clade I monkeypox to most people in the U.S. remains low, with no deaths associated with these cases and most people experiencing mild illness. Clade II has a death rate of less than 0.1%, while clade Ib has a death rate of less than 0.5%.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CDC continues to monitor both clade I and clade II monkeypox cases across the U.S. They are conducting surveillance testing to identify the clade of all specimens sent to their poxvirus laboratory. CDC also provides vaccination recommendations for people at risk and collaborates with public health departments to support prevention and clinical management efforts.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC's current situation report on monkeypox highlights ongoing outbreaks of both clade I and clade II monkeypox globally, with the U.S. experiencing more than 90 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I since November 2024. These cases are primarily linked to intimate or sexual contact, with a majority among men who have sex with men. The risk to most people in the U.S. from clade I remains low, and no deaths have been associated with these cases. The global clade II outbreak, which began in 2022, has caused over 100,000 cases in more than 120 countries, with a death rate of less than 0.1%. CDC is actively monitoring case counts, demographics, and disease severity, and is conducting surveillance testing to identify the clade of all specimens. They also provide vaccination recommendations for at-risk individuals and collaborate with public health departments to support prevention and clinical management efforts. The report emphasizes that clade I and II monkeypox can be spread, treated, and prevented similarly, and that domestic transmission of clade Ib is likely increasing in the U.S.

What to know There have been outbreaks of clade I monkeypox in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023. Since January 2024, nearly 60,000 confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported globally, including more than 150 deaths. Newer outbreaks in several Western European countries are likely related to this ongoing outbreak. Transmission dynamics are changing. Only a small proportion of exported clade I monkeypox cases worldwide this year have originated in Central or Eastern African countries. Recent travel-associated clade I monkeypox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib; there have been no deaths associated with these cases and available data have detailed relatively mild disease courses. Outbreak overview In the United States The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low. The risk to men who have sex with men is low to moderate. Clade I cases in the United States have increased in frequency since March 2026. As of October 2026, there have been more than 90 clade I monkeypox cases reported in at least 23 states plus Puerto Rico. The majority of these cases are among gay, bisexual, or other men who have sex with men. Many of these cases: Had recently traveled from areas associated with the outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa; Reported sexual contact during travel to parts of Western Europe where newer outbreaks are being reported; OR Reported sexual contact with people who had traveled from these areas. Since August 2026, an increasing proportion of clade I cases in the United States have been reported in individuals with no recent international travel or known links to people who had recently traveled. Cases with presumed domestic transmission have been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions, indicating a likely transition to sustained clade Ib transmission in the United States. CDC expects to see additional cases of both travel-related and domestically acquired cases of clade Ib occurring across the United States. Preventing Monkeypox While Traveling Learn where monkeypox is spreading and how to lower your risk of getting it during travel. In Central and Eastern Africa Clade Ia monkeypox outbreaks began impacting western areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2024. Available data indicate that clade Ia monkeypox has spread through sexual contact, regular household contact, and encounters with infected dead or live wild animals. Clade Ib monkeypox cases initially impacted eastern areas of DRC in late 2023. This subclade has driven much of the spread throughout Central and Eastern Africa and most travel-associated cases to other parts of the world. Available data indicate that these cases at first spread through heterosexual intimate or sexual contact between adults, then spread likely occurred within households, including to children. The disease spread in 2024 and 2025 to neighboring countries of DRC, only some of which are endemic for the virus that causes monkeypox, and sustained local spread occurred. Outside Central and Eastern Africa Several countries in other parts of Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America, as well as Australia, have confirmed clade I monkeypox cases mostly in travelers who'd recently been in areas with clade I outbreaks. To date, there have been more than 300 clade Ib cases in high-income countries, and no deaths have been reported. Several countries in Western Europe are reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to intimate or sexual exposure among men who have sex with men. We expect additional cases in Europe and the United States. For data since January 1, 2024, see 2022-24 Monkeypox (Monkeypox) Outbreak: Global Trends (shinyapps.io). Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. Clade I monkeypox and children Early in the Central and Eastern African outbreak that began in 2024, a high proportion of suspected cases in some areas were reported in children younger than 15 years of age. Historically, cases of monkeypox in children where monkeypox occurs regularly often happen after contact with wild animals that carry the disease. People then can spread the disease to close contacts, including in their households. The number of children with suspected monkeypox in this outbreak is probably due to spread within and between close households, the large number of younger people in affected countries, misdiagnosis of other diseases (such as measles), poor sanitary conditions, limited access to health services, and a high level of food insecurity and malnutrition. Based on what we know today, we don't expect to see the same sort of pattern in the United States for several reasons, including smaller household sizes, access to cleaning and disinfecting products, and improved access to medical care, equipment, and information about preventing spread while caring for patients. Notably, there are no consistent reports of schools as drivers of monkeypox transmission during any recent outbreaks. If cases of clade I monkeypox do happen in children the United States, CDC has clinical and public health guidance for reporting, testing, and effective case management. What CDC is doing CDC has been supporting DRC monkeypox research and response for more than 20 years. CDC and other U.S. government agencies have continued working in-country with partners in affected areas on disease surveillance, building local laboratory capacity, strengthening public health and laboratory workforce capacity, case investigation, case management, infection prevention and control, border health, and risk communication and community engagement. In the United States, CDC monitors both clade II and clade I monkeypox cases across the United States and follows surveillance reports to monitor for any changes in demographics, disease severity, or case counts by jurisdiction. CDC also performs surveillance testing to identify monkeypox clade for specimens sent to CDC's poxvirus laboratory. news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：暴发 于 2023 年底在中非和东非开始，自 2026 年 3 月起在美国的频率有所增加。截至 2026 年 10 月，暴发 仍...；地点与对象：中非和东非，特别是刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 和美国，至少 23 个州以及波多黎各报告了病例。在美国，大多数病例是同性恋、双性恋或其他男男性行为者。；事件：自 2023 年底以来，I 型猴痘 暴发 已在中非和东非发生，西欧国家较新的 暴发 可能与正在发生的 暴发 有关。在美国，自 2026 年 3 月以来，分支 I 猴痘病例有所增加，在多个司法管辖区观察到持续分支 Ib 传播 的转变。；影响与风险：自2024年1月起，全球已报告近60，000例I系猴痘确诊病例，包括超过150例死亡。在美国，截至2026年10月，已有23个州和波多黎各报告超过90例病例。对美国大多数人群的风险仍然较低，但对于男同性恋者则...；应对与不确定性：CDC 正在监控 暴发，为病例管理、检测和预防提供临床和公共卫生指导。I 型猴痘对美国大多数人造成的风险仍然很低，并且正在通过持续的数据收集和分析来跟踪其传播情况。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo ACAPS Briefing Note: Democratic Republic of Congo - Mpox outbreak affecting Kasaï province (13 October 2025) Format Situation Report Source ACAPS Posted 13 Oct 2026 Originally published 13 Oct 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.11 MB) CRISIS IMPACT OVERVIEW • On 16 September 2026, provincial authorities announced an mpox outbreak in Kasaï province, initially covering five health zones (7Sur7.cd 17/09/2026; mediacongo. net 17/09/2026). By 1 October, 1,017 cases and more than 24 deaths had been reported across all 18 of the province’s health zones (Actualite.cd 01/10/2026). • The declaration of a provincial mpox outbreak in Kasaï comes five months after the Government announced the end of a national mpox emergency designation; on 2 April, the Government announced a shift from emergency response to resilience, promoting community vigilance given the risk of resurgence (MSPHP 08/04/2026). The end of the emergency designation did not mean that transmission had ceased throughout the country, and available reporting does not establish whether the Kasaï outbreak is a result of continued local transmission or a new introduction into the province. • Earlier media reporting from 1–2 September quoting health sources identified Kambangoma and Mukwandjanga in Luebo health zone as the main affected locations, approximately 20km from the health zone coordination office. Authorities in Luebo were awaiting laboratory results from the National Biomedical Research Institute, indicating reliance on diagnostic support outside the health zone at that stage (ACP 01/09/2026; Radio Okapi 02/09/2026). The sources reviewed do not establish whether provincial testing arrangements have subsequently changed. • Hospital staff reported limited equipment and response resources from the outset. Suspected cases included infants aged two to three months. There were also reports of concerns about obtaining food and lodging during hospital care discouraging patients from seeking treatment (ACP 01/09/2026). • On 4 October, national health authorities deployed Rapid Intervention Teams to Tshikapa to support the Kasaï Provincial Health Division, particularly in Luebo. The mission focuses on epidemiological surveillance, the investigation and early detection of suspected cases, case management, and community awareness, while also reinforcing the operational capacity of local health teams (CongoCroissance 05/10/2026). • Kasaï is facing a simultaneous measles outbreak and suspected cases of yellow fever, increasing pressure on surveillance and health response capacity (WHO 31/08/2026; Beto 23/09/2026). At 9 October, no cases of Ebola had been reported in the province (CDC 09/10/2026). • On 26 September, an mpox case was confirmed in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province; by 29 September, there were five confirmed cases reported in Rwampara and Aru health zones of the province (MedAfrik Info Instagram 26/09/2026; mediacongo. net 01/10/2026; Reuters 25/09/2026). Earlier reports dating from July indicate nearly 4,000 cases confirmed in Sud-Kivu since the start of the year (mediacongo.net 23/07/2026). The available reporting does not establish whether cases in Ituri, Kasaï, and Sud-Kivu are linked to the same transmission chains. news.content_zh: 刚果民主共和国开赛省于 2026 年 9 月 16 日宣布爆发 猴痘 暴发,截至 2026 年 10 月 1 日,报告病例数为 1,017 例,死亡人数超过 24 人。暴发 最初影响了 5 个卫生区,其中 Luebo 卫生区的 Kambangoma 和 Mukwandjanga 是主要地点。当局依赖国家生物医学研究所的实验室结果来进行 诊断,医院工作人员指出资源有限。国家卫生当局于 2026 年 10 月 4 日向奇卡帕部署了快速干预小组,以支持当地的努力。暴发 与麻疹和黄热病 暴发 同时发生,增加了卫生系统的压力。截至 2026 年 10 月 9 日,该省尚未报告埃博拉病例。消息来源并未确认 暴发 是由于当地 传播 还是新传入的,并且 2026 年 4 月国家 猴痘 紧急指定的结束并不一定表明 传播 的停止。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs Order DNA Kits Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram When monkeypox virus, now widely referred to as MPOX, began spreading beyond its traditional African strongholds in 2022, the world was forced to reconsider a disease long classified as a neglected tropical condition. What had once been a largely localized public health concern rapidly became a global problem, exposing glaring gaps in preparedness, therapeutics, and public awareness. Although vaccines originally developed against smallpox offer some cross-protection, most of the world’s population remains unvaccinated, whether because of limited availability, hesitancy, or simple lack of awareness. More striking still is the absence of any officially approved drug specifically targeting MPOX. A new computational study published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases by Sabkat Mahmud, Alvira Ajadee, and colleagues addresses this therapeutic vacuum by combining host transcriptomics, network biology, and molecular simulation to map the disease’s inner workings and to nominate existing drugs that might be redirected against it. The research team’s strategy rested on a deceptively simple premise: rather than studying the virus in isolation, they examined how human cells respond to infection. Viruses are obligate hijackers, and the genes a host cell switches on or off during infection often reveal the molecular levers the pathogen pulls. The investigators mined three independent transcriptomic profile datasets comparing gene expression in MPOX patients against healthy controls. By intersecting the results across datasets, they filtered out noise and arrived at 166 common host differentially expressed genes, or hDEGs, that consistently distinguish infected individuals from uninfected ones. Of these, 75 genes were upregulated, meaning their activity increased during infection, while 91 were downregulated, suggesting suppression of functions the virus may find inconvenient. Identifying differentially expressed genes is only the first step in untangling a disease process. To separate genuine drivers from incidental bystanders, the team turned to protein-protein interaction network analysis, a technique that maps the web of physical and functional contacts among the proteins encoded by the altered genes. Genes sitting at highly connected nodes of such networks often exert outsized influence on cellular behavior. From this analysis, six top-ranked host key genes emerged as potential MPOX-causing genes: ALB, HSP90AA1, CDH1, PTPRC, IGF1, and ABL1. Each tells a plausible story. ALB encodes serum albumin, the body’s most abundant plasma protein and a marker of liver function and fluid balance. HSP90AA1 is a molecular chaperone that stabilizes many client proteins, including those involved in immune signaling. CDH1 produces E-cadherin, a cell adhesion molecule critical to maintaining epithelial barriers, the very front line that poxviruses breach. PTPRC, better known as CD45, is a tyrosine phosphatase essential for lymphocyte activation, pointing to immune cell involvement. IGF1 governs growth factor signaling, and ABL1 is a kinase with well-characterized roles in cell proliferation and DNA damage responses. Order DNA Kits Discover more Drugs Drug Save on Rx drugs drug With these six hub genes in hand, the researchers performed functional enrichment analysis to determine which biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and signaling pathways the genes collectively implicate. Such enrichment analysis asks whether a set of genes is overrepresented in known functional categories compared with what chance would predict. The results painted a coherent picture of MPOX pathogenesis, highlighting processes tied to immune response regulation, epithelial integrity, and metabolic adaptation. The team also extended the analysis to KEGG pathways, a curated database of molecular interaction and reaction networks, which helped situate the hub genes within broader cellular circuits. Complementing this, a regulatory network analysis identified transcription factors and microRNAs that potentially control the expression of the key genes, adding another layer of mechanistic insight. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on or off, while microRNAs are small RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression after transcription; mapping these regulators helps explain how the observed expression changes might arise during infection. Order DNA Kits The second half of the study pivoted from understanding the disease to treating it. Rather than waiting years for a novel antiviral to be discovered and tested, the team pursued drug repurposing, the strategy of finding new uses for approved or well-characterized compounds. Repurposing offers a substantial speed advantage because existing drugs already have established safety profiles, manufacturing routes, and, in many cases, clinical experience in humans. The researchers screened candidate molecules against the proteins implicated in MPOX using molecular docking, a computational method that predicts how strongly and in what orientation a small molecule binds to a target protein’s binding site. From this screen, five top-ranked drug candidates emerged: Tecovirimat, Beclabuvir, Maraviroc, Raltegravir, and Brincidofovir. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Genes Several of these nominations carry intriguing logic. Tecovirimat is an antiviral originally developed against smallpox that inhibits the VP37 envelope protein of orthopoxviruses, the viral family that includes monkeypox, and it has already seen emergency use during recent outbreaks. Brincidofovir is a lipid conjugate of cidofovir designed to accumulate in cells and disrupt viral DNA replication, and it too carries orthopoxvirus indications. Maraviroc, by contrast, is an HIV entry inhibitor that blocks the CCR5 receptor on immune cells, while Raltegravir is an HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor, and Beclabuvir is an investigational hepatitis C NS5A inhibitor. That compounds developed for entirely different pathogens dock favorably onto host or viral proteins relevant to MPOX illustrates the core promise of repurposing: molecular interfaces evolved for one purpose can sometimes be exploited for another. Computational docking alone can be misleading, however, because a molecule that fits a binding site in a static snapshot may fail to maintain that interaction under the dynamic conditions of a living cell. To address this, the team evaluated the pharmacokinetic credentials of all five candidates using ADME/T analysis, which assesses absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, alongside drug-likeness filters that compare molecular properties against those of successful oral medicines. The candidates passed these evaluations with favorable profiles, suggesting that, in principle, they could reach their targets in the body at effective concentrations without unacceptable toxicity. The strongest computational evidence came from molecular dynamics simulations, which model the physical motion of atoms over time to test whether a drug-protein complex remains stable in a realistic, fluctuating environment. The researchers ran 100-nanosecond simulations of the three most promising complexes: ALB bound to Tecovirimat, CDH1 bound to Maraviroc, and PPARG bound to Beclabuvir. PPARG, the nuclear receptor targeted by Beclabuvir in this analysis, adds an interesting metabolic dimension to the proposed mechanism. Throughout the simulations, the team tracked root-mean-square deviation, or RMSD, which measures how far the protein structure drifts from its starting conformation, and root-mean-square fluctuation, or RMSF, which quantifies how much individual residues wiggle locally. They also computed binding free energies using the MM-GBSA method, which estimates the thermodynamic favorability of the drug-protein interaction. All three complexes demonstrated strong binding stability across these metrics, indicating that the docked poses were not artifacts of a single frozen structure but held up under sustained atomic motion. The convergence of transcriptomic evidence, network analysis, docking, pharmacokinetic screening, and dynamic simulation gives the study an unusually complete computational arc, moving from disease mechanism to therapeutic nomination within a single framework. The identification of host key genes such as ALB, CDH1, and PTPRC may also inform diagnostic development, since consistently dysregulated host transcripts can serve as biomarkers distinguishing MPOX from other febrile illnesses, a persistent challenge in regions where poxvirus, malaria, and other infections overlap clinically. Yet the authors are careful to frame their findings as a starting point rather than a conclusion. Every result in the study, from the 166 differentially expressed genes to the stability of the simulated drug complexes, derives from computational inference and must be validated experimentally in the laboratory before it can inform clinical practice. Docking scores do not guarantee efficacy in infected cells, and transcriptomic correlations do not prove causation. Still, in a landscape where no approved MPOX drug exists and vaccine coverage remains sparse, computational pipelines like this one offer a rapid, systematic way to prioritize which existing molecules deserve the first laboratory look. As MPOX continues to circulate globally, such approaches may shorten the path from genomic data to actionable therapeutics, turning the growing archive of patient transcriptomes into a roadmap for fighting a disease the world can no longer afford to neglect.
