news.content_title: South Africa confirms four new mpox cases as Western Cape remains hardest hit
news.content: South Africa has recorded four additional mpox infections, bringing the national total to 26 since the beginning of 2026, with the Western Cape accounting for the overwhelming majority of confirmed cases, Cape {town} Etc reports. The Department of Health has urged the public to remain alert to symptoms and seek medical attention early, as health authorities continue efforts to identify infections and prevent further transmission. Of the 26 confirmed cases, 18 have been recorded in the Western Cape, highlighting the importance of continued monitoring and public awareness in the province. The latest figures show that mpox cases have been detected in five provinces, with the Western Cape reporting significantly more infections than the rest of the country. Gauteng has recorded three cases, while the Eastern Cape and Free State have reported two each. KwaZulu-Natal has one confirmed case. According to the Department of Health , 16 of the Western Cape’s 18 cases are linked to local transmission. The other two involved foreign nationals who contracted the virus outside South Africa. The figures indicate that local transmission is a key concern for health authorities, making early detection and the identification of people who may have been exposed important parts of the response. Who is most affected? Of the 26 people diagnosed with mpox, 25 are reportedly male. Their ages range from 23 to 50, with a median age of 37. Laboratory information on the virus’s clade and lineage is available for 17 cases. Of these, 13 are associated with Clade Ib and four with Clade IIb. These classifications help health authorities understand which variants are involved in the outbreak and support efforts to monitor how the virus is spreading. Symptoms to watch for Department of Health spokesperson Foster Mohale has urged people not to ignore possible signs of infection. ‘We urge members of the public to remain vigilant and seek healthcare promptly if they develop symptoms such as a rash, fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes or fatigue.’ – Foster Mohale, Department of Health spokesperson Mpox can spread through close physical contact , including skin-to-skin contact with an infected person. Contact with contaminated bedding, towels, clothing and other personal items can also pose a risk. Anyone who develops a suspicious rash or other symptoms should seek medical advice, particularly if they have recently been in close contact with someone who may have the virus. People who have been exposed to a confirmed or suspected case are advised to inform healthcare workers and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. ‘If symptoms develop, they should avoid close contact with others and seek medical attention,’ Mohale said. Prevention remains a priority The Department of Health says mpox is preventable and treatable, and is urging South Africans to take precautions to reduce the risk of infection. Avoiding close contact with anyone who has an mpox-like rash and not sharing personal items with an infected person are among the recommended measures. Healthcare workers have also been urged to remain alert to possible cases and follow infection prevention and control procedures when assessing patients. The department is working with the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) , provincial health authorities and other stakeholders to strengthen surveillance, identify new infections and trace contacts. With most confirmed cases concentrated in the Western Cape, public awareness and timely reporting of symptoms remain important tools in limiting further spread. Celebrities Useful Tips World News Celebrities Useful Tips World News World News 0 Mpox Vaccine Slashes Infection Risk by 82%: Real-World Data Details Protection Levels By Сollin RuggPosted onOctober 17, 2026 Time to Read:-words A complete two-dose vaccination schedule provides robust protection against mpox transmission and severe systemic illness. Completing a two-dose course of the mpox vaccine slashes the risk of infection by 82 per cent, providing a substantial protective barrier against the virus. Furthermore, clinical findings reveal that vaccinated individuals who encounter breakthrough infections are 87 per cent less likely to experience viral spread across other parts of the body. With ongoing surveillance surrounding evolving viral lineages such as clade 1b, international public health authorities continue tracking how existing immunisation strategies perform against severe disease. The core protection offered by the current two-dose regimen significantly restricts outward transmission to close contacts and sexual partners, directly shielding vulnerable networks from sustained infection chains. The biological mechanisms behind this defence explain why full-course immunisation remains vital for high-risk demographics. Clinical Protection Levels and Viral Containment The standard immunisation protocol relies on priming the immune system with two separate inoculations to generate sustained neutralising antibodies. Laboratory and epidemiological evaluations show that completing both doses provides the decisive threshold required to suppress active replication. When an individual contracts the virus after completing their inoculations, systemic dissemination remains tightly suppressed. The 87 per cent reduction in viral dissemination prevents lesions from multiplying across multiple anatomical zones, such as the trunk, genital area, and limbs, transforming what could be an extensive illness into a mild, contained presentation. Vaccination provides a highly effective protective barrier by reducing infection risk and limiting bodily spread. Understanding these biological barriers highlights why a partial, single-dose course fails to deliver long-term protection against exposure. Key Metrics: Two-Dose Vaccine Performance Clinical data demonstrate a marked distinction between individuals who receive complete protection and those left unprotected during an exposure event. Metric Observed Impact Overall Infection Risk Reduction 82% reduction after two doses Suppression of Bodily Viral Spread 87% lower risk of systemic dissemination Dosing Schedule Requirement Two full doses required for peak efficacy Primary Clinical Outcome Prevention of widespread rash and systemic illness These clinical metrics directly challenge several widespread misconceptions regarding how the virus behaves across communities. Myth vs Reality: Public Misconceptions on Transmission and Immunity A widespread assumption suggests that receiving a single vaccine jab offers adequate lifetime defence against viral transmission. The reality is that antibody titers remain suboptimal without the mandatory second dose, leaving the immune system vulnerable to breakthrough infections when facing high-risk exposure. Another prevalent myth claims that vaccination completely eliminates the chance of acquiring a localised infection. In practice, immunised individuals may still encounter the virus, but the immune response rapidly neutralises systemic propagation, effectively preventing secondary transmission chains to partners. To maximise personal protection and safeguard partners, public health officials advise clear preventive steps. Recommended Protection and Response Protocol Complete the Regimen: Ensure both doses of the vaccine are administered according to recommended health service intervals. Monitor for Symptoms: Look out for early indicators such as fever, persistent sore throat, or localised rashes across the genital area and limbs. Seek Prompt Assessment: Contact local sexual health clinics or specialised health hotlines immediately upon noticing unexplained lesions. Isolate and Trace: Refrain from close physical contact and assist health services with partner notification to rapidly halt onward transmission. Maintaining active vigilance and ensuring timely access to clinical services ensures community transmission remains strictly contained. 💡 Staying informed about full immunisation schedules ensures strong defence against emerging viral risks. 🔍 Check your local clinic or sexual health service to verify your eligibility for the recommended two-dose course. 👇 Share your experiences or questions in the comments below to help keep the wider community informed. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health From One Health Surveillance to Mpox and Prions: New Research Tracks the Rise of Emerging Diseases by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 From One Health Surveillance to Mpox and Prions: New Research Tracks the Rise of Emerging Diseases Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A sweeping new collection of studies published in Frontiers in Tropical Diseases is offering a multidimensional view of how infectious diseases emerge, re-emerge, and ripple across ecosystems, economies, and public health systems. The research topic, titled “Exploring the Dynamics of Emerging and Re-Emerging Diseases: From Origins to Impact, Volume II,” brings together work spanning tropical disease surveillance, molecular diagnostics, arboviral outbreaks, SARS-CoV-2 reinfection, prion disease, and Mpox-HIV co-infection, painting a picture of a world where the boundaries between human, animal, and environmental health are increasingly porous. At the heart of the collection is a call to rethink how the world detects and responds to disease threats before they spiral into crises. A review by Abdulsalam and colleagues argues that effective surveillance under a “One Health” framework must be proactive rather than reactive, incorporating climate intelligence and addressing the behavioral and social drivers of disease. The authors emphasize that technologies such as artificial intelligence, genomic sequencing, environmental biosensors, and mobile health platforms are dramatically enhancing the speed and scalability of detection, response, and prevention of cross-species transmission. They also stress the need for interdisciplinary education, policy support, and real-time data sharing to build system-wide resilience, recommending that local communities be involved in shaping context-specific surveillance strategies in ecologically sensitive tropical regions. Complementing this systems-level perspective, a study by Iqrar and colleagues developed and validated a novel multiplex PCR assay capable of simultaneously detecting Anaplasma, Babesia, and Theileria pathogens at the genus level in captive wild ungulates. The researchers designed primer pairs targeting the 18S ribosomal RNA gene for piroplasmids, generating products of 178 base pairs for Theileria and 479 base pairs for Babesia, while a separate primer pair targeting the 16S rRNA gene produced an expected 318 base pair product for Anaplasma. Testing blood samples from 60 captive Gazella bennettii and Axis porcinus across wildlife parks and zoos in Punjab, Pakistan, the team found an overall hemoparasite prevalence of 66.66 percent, with sequencing confirming the results and offering a valuable complementary tool for routine, accurate detection in endangered species. Discover more Find Treatments Check Symptoms Track Outbreaks Study Biology health The collection also ventures into the unsettling territory of prion diseases. A clinical case report by Kotkowski and colleagues details the evaluation of a 72-year-old hunter who developed progressive rapid dementia and startle myoclonus after extensive exposure to cervids in a chronic wasting disease-endemic region. During hospitalization, the patient developed posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed cortical ribboning and diffusion restriction in the basal ganglia. Cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, including RT-QuIC, total tau, and the 14-3-3 protein, along with post-mortem neuropathology, confirmed sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease of the MM1 subtype. The authors use the case to raise pointed questions about zoonotic surveillance, particularly for hunters with prolonged exposure to wildlife in regions where chronic wasting disease circulates. Shifting to viral threats, Kuang and colleagues examined the epidemiological characteristics and transmission dynamics of Mpox-HIV co-infection in a low-incidence setting in Qinghai Province, China. The patient, a man who has sex with men, presented with a fever of 39.4 degrees Celsius, and recovery of mpox virus nucleic acid was confirmed from a nasopharyngeal swab. Genomic characterization identified the virus as clade IIb, C.1.1 sub-lineage, with the full designation B.1.3.1.1. Notably, the patient had no history of international travel, leading the authors to conclude that the most likely route of exposure was high-risk sexual contact within a local social or sexual network. This finding suggests that silent transmission may already be occurring in regions previously considered low-incidence, exposing systemic gaps in surveillance, diagnosis, and response. The COVID-19 pandemic’s long tail is also examined. Makam and colleagues retrospectively analyzed reinfection data from patients during the second and third waves of the pandemic, finding that of 458 participants, 62, or 13.54 percent, who had a primary infection were confirmed to have been reinfected. Among these, 60 participants, or 13 percent, were asymptomatic, while 398, or 87 percent, were symptomatic, with fever being the most frequently observed symptom during both primary and reinfection episodes. The study also identified a statistically significant association between infection status and vomiting symptoms, adding to the growing body of evidence on how reinfection dynamics and vaccination status interact. Perhaps the most geographically expansive contribution comes from Carrero and Mosquera, who reviewed the re-emergence of arboviruses across the Andean-Amazonian corridor in Latin America. Analyzing datasets on vector-borne diseases from selected countries between 2023 and 2026, they documented the persistence of malaria in Amazonian areas alongside a sustained increase in arboviral infections such as yellow fever, dengue, and chikungunya. Colombia recorded 132 confirmed human cases of yellow fever between 2024 and 2025, while Ecuador registered 65 deaths from 37,840 cases of dengue. Signs of yellow fever re-emergence were also observed in Venezuela during 2025 and 2026, attributed to sylvatic cycles of the virus. Discover more Get Health Tips Health Read Med Journals public health Public Health The authors attribute the re-emergence of these arboviruses to a convergence of ecological, social, and health factors, including poor health education, vaccine hesitancy, limited access to health services, the infodemic, and weaknesses in epidemiological surveillance and vector control. Their findings underscore how fragile public health infrastructure, when combined with environmental change and human mobility, can create conditions ripe for pathogens to resurge even in regions where they were previously contained. Together, the studies in this collection offer a deeper understanding of the ecological, genetic, environmental, and socioeconomic factors that drive the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases. They also highlight the cascading effects these diseases exert on public health, societies, and economies, reinforcing the argument that no single discipline or nation can address these threats in isolation. As the editorial’s authors make clear, the path forward demands sustained cross-sectoral integration, investment in molecular and genomic tools, and a willingness to confront the social and behavioral dimensions of disease transmission. From the jungles of the Amazon to the wildlife parks of Punjab and the clinics of Qinghai, the message is consistent: the next emerging disease is not a question of if, but when, and the world’s surveillance systems must be ready. The authors emphasize that technologies such as artificial intelligence, genomic sequencing, environmental biosensors, and mobile health platforms are dramatically enhancing the speed and scalability of detection, response, and prevention of cross-species transmission. They also stress the need for interdisciplinary education, policy support, and real-time data sharing to build system-wide resilience, recommending that local communities be involved in shaping context-specific surveillance strategies in ecologically sensitive tropical regions. Complementing this systems-level perspective, a study by Iqrar and colleagues developed and validated a novel multiplex PCR assay capable of simultaneously detecting Anaplasma, Babesia, and Theileria pathogens at the genus level in captive wild ungulates. The researchers designed primer pairs targeting the 18S ribosomal RNA gene for piroplasmids, generating products of 178 base pairs for Theileria and 479 base pairs for Babesia, while a separate primer pair targeting the 16S rRNA gene produced an expected 318 base pair product for Anaplasma. Testing blood samples from 60 captive Gazella bennettii and Axis porcinus across wildlife parks and zoos in Punjab, Pakistan, the team found an overall hemoparasite prevalence of 66.66 percent, with sequencing confirming the results and offering a valuable complementary tool for routine, accurate detection in endangered species. Discover more Find Treatments Check Symptoms Track Outbreaks Study Biology health The collection also ventures into the unsettling territory of prion diseases. A clinical case report by Kotkowski and colleagues details the evaluation of a 72-year-old hunter who developed progressive rapid dementia and startle myoclonus after extensive exposure to cervids in a chronic wasting disease-endemic region. During hospitalization, the patient developed posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed cortical ribboning and diffusion restriction in the basal ganglia. Cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, including RT-QuIC, total tau, and the 14-3-3 protein, along with post-mortem neuropathology, confirmed sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease of the MM1 subtype. The authors use the case to raise pointed questions about zoonotic surveillance, particularly for hunters with prolonged exposure to wildlife in regions where chronic wasting disease circulates. Shifting to viral threats, Kuang and colleagues examined the epidemiological characteristics and transmission dynamics of Mpox-HIV co-infection in a low-incidence setting in Qinghai Province, China. The patient, a man who has sex with men, presented with a fever of 39.4 degrees Celsius, and recovery of mpox virus nucleic acid was confirmed from a nasopharyngeal swab. Genomic characterization identified the virus as clade IIb, C.1.1 sub-lineage, with the full designation B.1.3.1.1. Notably, the patient had no history of international travel, leading the authors to conclude that the most likely route of exposure was high-risk sexual contact within a local social or sexual network. This finding suggests that silent transmission may already be occurring in regions previously considered low-incidence, exposing systemic gaps in surveillance, diagnosis, and response. The COVID-19 pandemic’s long tail is also examined. Makam and colleagues retrospectively analyzed reinfection data from patients during the second and third waves of the pandemic, finding that of 458 participants, 62, or 13.54 percent, who had a primary infection were confirmed to have been reinfected. Among these, 60 participants, or 13 percent, were asymptomatic, while 398, or 87 percent, were symptomatic, with fever being the most frequently observed symptom during both primary and reinfection episodes. The study also identified a statistically significant association between infection status and vomiting symptoms, adding to the growing body of evidence on how reinfection dynamics and vaccination status interact. Perhaps the most geographically expansive contribution comes from Carrero and Mosquera, who reviewed the re-emergence of arboviruses across the Andean-Amazonian corridor in Latin America. Analyzing datasets on vector-borne diseases from selected countries between 2023 and 2026, they documented the persistence of malaria in Amazonian areas alongside a sustained increase in arboviral infections such as yellow fever, dengue, and chikungunya. Colombia recorded 132 confirmed human cases of yellow fever between 2024 and 2025, while Ecuador registered 65 deaths from 37,840 cases of dengue. Signs of yellow fever re-emergence were also observed in Venezuela during 2025 and 2026, attributed to sylvatic cycles of the virus. Discover more Get Health Tips Health Read Med Journals public health Public Health The authors attribute the re-emergence of these arboviruses to a convergence of ecological, social, and health factors, including poor health education, vaccine hesitancy, limited access to health services, the infodemic, and weaknesses in epidemiological surveillance and vector control. Their findings underscore how fragile public health infrastructure, when combined with environmental change and human mobility, can create conditions ripe for pathogens to resurge even in regions where they were previously contained. Together, the studies in this collection offer a deeper understanding of the ecological, genetic, environmental, and socioeconomic factors that drive the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases. They also highlight the cascading effects these diseases exert on public health, societies, and economies, reinforcing the argument that no single discipline or nation can address these threats in isolation. As the editorial’s authors make clear, the path forward demands sustained cross-sectoral integration, investment in molecular and genomic tools, and a willingness to confront the social and behavioral dimensions of disease transmission. From the jungles of the Amazon to the wildlife parks of Punjab and the clinics of Qinghai, the message is consistent: the next emerging disease is not a question of if, but when, and the world’s surveillance systems must be ready. news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 17 日发表的一项新研究探讨了中国青海省低 发病率 环境中 猴痘-HIV 混合感染的流行病学特征和 发病率 动态。这项研究是关于新发疾病的更广泛收集的一部分,重点关注一名与男性发生性行为并出现 39.4 摄氏度发烧的男性。基因组特征证实该病毒属于进化枝 IIb,C.1.1 亚系,最可能的暴露途径是本地网络内的高风险性接触。作者指出,该病例表明沉默的 发病率 可能发生在先前被认为低 发病率 的区域,突出了 监测、诊断 和响应的系统性差距。该研究强调了主动疾病监测和整合基因组测序等技术以加强检测和预防工作的重要性。它还呼吁采取跨学科方法和社区参与,制定针对生态敏感地区疾病 监测 的具体策略。

news.content: Language SIGN IN USER Your account Sign out Radio TV Ask China Newsletters RSS EXPLORE MORE English Español Français العربية Русский Documentary CCTV+ Home China World World Asia-Pacific Middle East Europe Americas Africa Politics Business Opinions Sci-Tech Culture Sports Travel Nature Picture Video Live Documentary World 2026.10.16 10:57 GMT+8 Russia investigates suspected monkeypox outbreak near Moscow Updated 2026.10.16 10:57 GMT+8 CGTN Russian health authorities have launched an epidemiological investigation and implemented comprehensive anti-epidemic measures following a suspected monkeypox outbreak in the Moscow Region, officials announced on October 15. According to a public statement released by the Federal Service for Oversight of Consumer Protection and Welfare (Rospotrebnadzor), five people who came into contact with a suspected monkeypox carrier have been hospitalized for medical observation and diagnostic testing. A monkeypox test kit at the State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology Vector in Novosibirsk, Russia. /CFP The Moscow Region Ministry of Health confirmed that all five patients are in satisfactory condition and show no pronounced clinical symptoms. Authorities said emergency containment measures, including contact tracing, laboratory testing and widespread disinfection, were implemented immediately. Rospotrebnadzor said health officials are using advanced diagnostic systems developed in-house to ensure the rapid detection of the virus. While testing is underway, officials emphasized that no new cases have been confirmed. A syringe lies on a vaccination card marked "Mpox vaccination." /CFP This development follows earlier reported cases in the area. In February 2026, health authorities confirmed a monkeypox case in Domodedovo. A close contact was subsequently hospitalized, and two tourists returning to St. Petersburg from Thailand were later diagnosed with the disease. Monkeypox is a viral zoonotic disease. Initial symptoms in humans include fever, headaches, muscle aches, back pain and swollen lymph nodes. These may be followed by extensive rashes on the face and body. While most infected people recover within a few weeks, some may develop severe illness or die. Illustrative image. (Source: Getty Images) Five people were hospitalized in Russia’s Moscow region after contact with a person suspected of having mpox, according to Interfax on October 15. The Moscow region Health Ministry confirmed the hospitalizations to Interfax on October 15, reporting that all five individuals were placed under medical observation. Authorities collected samples for laboratory testing to determine whether they had contracted the virus. We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field. DONATE NOW The ministry noted that all five patients were in satisfactory condition and showed no clinical symptoms of mpox. Their test results had not been disclosed, while the suspected infection that prompted their hospitalization remained unconfirmed. Later on October 15, Russia’s consumer health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, announced that it had launched an epidemiological investigation into the suspected case. The agency confirmed that five contacts were hospitalized and that disinfection measures had been ordered. "Specialists from Rospotrebnadzor's Moscow region office immediately launched a sanitary and epidemiological investigation," the agency stated, as reported by Interfax. Officials added that they were identifying additional contacts and implementing measures to prevent further transmission. Read more Category War in Ukraine Russia Hides Potential Pneumonic Plague Outbreak After Fatal Lab Breach Oct 04, 2026 12:45 The development follows several confirmed mpox infections in Russia earlier in 2026. On February 15, RBC reported, citing Rospotrebnadzor, that two men returning from Thailand had tested positive for the virus in St. Petersburg. Both were hospitalized, while authorities placed their contacts under medical observation. The suspected mpox case follows public health concerns in Siberia, where an alleged plague outbreak in the Irkutsk region drew international attention earlier in October. Laboratory worker Darya Shipilova, 28, died on October 2 after reportedly breaking a test tube containing live bacteria at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and hundreds of her contacts were placed in quarantine. Russian authorities attributed her death to unidentified pneumonia and denied that an outbreak was occurring. Unconfirmed reports of a second death emerged on October 6, while Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan tightened health controls. news.content: Exclusive Nation business life opinion Russian war Nation Dear reader! This article will be available right after an advertisement. Five quarantined in Moscow Oblast over suspected mpox as sanitary probe begins October 16, 2026, 07:39 AM 208 World Five residents of Moscow Oblast were placed under strict three-week quarantine (Photo: REUTERS/Anastasia Barashkova) Five residents were hospitalized under quarantine in Moscow Oblast with suspected mpox (Monkeypox virus), Russian state media reported on Oct. 16. The hospitalized patients include three men and two women aged between 21 and 35. Investigators believe the individuals came into direct contact with an infected carrier on Oct. 10, later seeking medical attention. All five patients have been placed into an obligatory three-week clinical quarantine. Read also: U.S. embassy issues health alert over Russia plague risk The regional directorate of consumer and health regulator Rospotrebnadzor verified the incident, confirming that a sanitary-epidemiological investigation is underway and formal orders for comprehensive localized disinfection have been executed. Ad Russia’s Ministry of Health claimed the patients remain in satisfactory clinical condition and currently exhibit no overt symptoms of the virus. However, Russian media noted that laboratory diagnostic samples have not yet been processed, leaving the mpox diagnosis officially unconfirmed. Suspicious Biological Incidents Across Russia Read also: Cause of Russian plague lab worker’s death still unknown Lethal infection at Siberian anti-plague institute: The Moscow Oblast quarantine follows the death of 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, a laboratory specialist at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk Oblast. Russian independent media reported that on Sept. 25, Shipilova accidentally broke a test tube containing the pathogen for pneumonic plague. She was hospitalized with severe pneumonia on Sept. 29 and died overnight into Oct. 2. Covert quarantine orders in Irkutsk: Following Shipilova's death, Russian authorities enacted strict containment protocols across her research laboratory and adjoining medical clinics, locking down staff inside the facilities for three days and placing roughly 200 secondary contacts under surveillance. Officially, Russian authorities claimed Shipilova succumbed to "pneumonia of unknown origin" and vehemently denied any plague breach. U.S. intelligence and diplomatic scrutiny: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the U.S. State Department, and allied agencies launched inquiries to determine the circumstances surrounding Shipilova’s death and the subsequent hospital quarantines in Siberia. On Oct. 5, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly described the Siberian outbreak as a "big problem for Russia" and offered technical assistance, subsequently announcing plans for a direct telephone call with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin to address the suspected plague incident. The military war may be swinging in our favor, but the information war continues. Just as an army needs soldiers, so does a free society need its journalists to ensure that people have access to honest, trustworthy voices to understand the world around them. news.content_zh: 据俄罗斯官方媒体 2026 年 10 月 16 日报道,俄罗斯莫斯科州有 5 人因疑似 猴痘 感染而接受严格的三周隔离。这些患者包括 3 名男性和 2 名女性,年龄在 21 岁至 35 岁之间,于 10 月 10 日直接接触受感染的携带者后入院。俄罗斯消费者和卫生监管局地区管理局确认了这一隔离情况,并启动了卫生流行病学调查进行排查,并采取局部消毒措施。然而,由于实验室样本尚未处理,猴痘 诊断 仍未得到证实。目前,患者临床状况良好,无明显症状。该事件发生前,伊尔库茨克州一名 28 岁的实验室专家不小心打破了含有肺鼠疫病原体的试管,导致死亡。俄罗斯当局否认有任何与鼠疫有关的违规行为,而疾病预防控制中心和美国国务院已对死亡情况和随后的隔离情况展开调查。该报告强调了持续存在的公共卫生问题以及需要进一步调查以确认 猴痘 的存在。

news.content: Sunday, October 18, 2026 News Crime and Courts South Africa Africa World BRICS Education Energy Environment Feel Good Government at Work Opinion LGE2026 Politics Opinion Opinion News Politics Entertainment Lifestyle Tech Sport Business Jobs Economy Property Window on China Hybrid Working Entertainment Celebrity News Streaming Movies Music Books Whats On Joburg Durban Cape Town Pretoria Opinion Lifestyle Health Beauty Fashion Food Relationships Parenting Competitions Opinion Travel Local International Tech Software and Internet Esports Opinion Sport Soccer PSL Rugby Cricket MMA HOLLYWOODBETS iGAMING Opinion Horse Racing Motoring Reviews Launches Industry News Motorsport News South Africa Health department sounds alarm as four new Mpox cases push SA total to 26 Xolile Mtembu|Published 13 hours ago Ask AI 2min The Department of Health has issued a warning after four new mpox cases were confirmed in South Africa, bringing the national tally to 26. With 16 Western Cape cases linked to local transmission, authorities are urging people to avoid close contact with infected individuals and monitor symptoms for 21 days after exposure. Image: FILE South Africa has recorded four new Mpox cases, pushing the national tally to 26 since the beginning of the year, with the Western Cape accounting for the overwhelming majority of infections. The Department of Health has urged the public to remain vigilant, recognise the warning signs and seek medical attention promptly to help prevent further transmission of the virus. Spokesperson Foster Mohale confirmed the increase, saying the latest cases had raised the cumulative number of laboratory-confirmed infections from 22 to 26. Western Cape accounts for 18 infections Of the 26 confirmed cases recorded since January 1, 2026, the Western Cape has reported 18, followed by Gauteng with three, the Eastern Cape and Free State with two each, and KwaZulu-Natal with one. Two of the Western Cape cases involved foreign nationals visiting South Africa and were classified as imported infections. The remaining 16 were linked to local transmission. The department said 25 of the 26 people diagnosed with mpox were male, with ages ranging from 23 to 50. The median age was 37. Clade and lineage information was available for 17 cases. Of these, 13 were associated with Clade Ib and four with Clade IIb. Mohale urged people to take precautions and seek help if they suspected they had contracted the virus. “The department urges members of the public to remain vigilant and to seek healthcare promptly if they develop symptoms such as a rash, fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes or fatigue,” he said. Public warned about close contact Mpox is a viral infection that can spread through close contact with an infected person. The department advised anyone who had been in close contact with a confirmed or suspected case to notify healthcare workers and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. People who develop symptoms should avoid close contact with others and seek medical attention. The public has also been warned against close, skin-to-skin contact with anyone who has a rash suspected to be linked to mpox. Sharing personal belongings, including bedding, towels and clothing, with affected individuals should be avoided. Mohale emphasised that people who may have been exposed should monitor their health carefully. “Individuals who have been in close contact with a confirmed or suspected mpox case should inform healthcare workers and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days,” he said. news.content: EPAPER LIVE TV DAWNNEWS URDU Images Herald Aurora CityFM89 Advertise Events Supplements Careers Obituaries Dawn E-Paper | October 19, 2026 Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Home Latest US-Iran War Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Search Search Subscribe to notifications Get the latest news and updates from Dawn Not Now Allow Notifications Infant boy tests positive for mpox in Sindh as tally rises to 94 Faiza Ilyas Published October 15, 2026 Email Story Your Name * Recipient Email * Send Email Cancel 0 FILE PHOTO: A test tube labelled "Mpox virus positive" is held in this illustration taken August 20, 2024. — Reuters/File comments Join our Whatsapp Channel KARACHI: The city reported its first mpox case involving an infant boy on Wednesday evening as the total number of people affected by the disease in Sindh this year rose to 94. Sources said the 40-day-old baby boy was currently under treatment at the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital & Research Centre (SIDH&RC). The parents are residents of Landhi. Speaking to Dawn on condition of anonymity, a senior SIDH&RC doctor said that the baby boy had initially been examined at a clinic in Landhi four to five days ago, after which he developed fever and rashes all over the body. “The parents took him to a Korangi hospital, from where he was referred to us. He is stable but restless,” he said, adding that 23 mpox patients, including the latest case, had reported at the hospital this year so far. The sources said that two mpox patients, one with severe lung illness and the other with chronic kidney disease, had died at the hospital over the past few weeks. In hospital records, however, their causes of death were attributed to their chronic illnesses rather than mpox. Early this month, the Provincial Disease Surveillance and Response Unit released data showing 11 deaths from mpox this year. It showed that Karachi is the most mpox-affected city with 28 cases, followed by 22 in Khairpur and nine in Sukkur. The monthly trend showed that April saw the largest number of cases (31) this year, followed by September (20) and August (17). Seventy cases involved male patients, and the most affected age group was 30 to 39 years. Twenty-three cases involved children aged zero to nine years across the province, and 18 cases involved adults aged 20-29. Seventy-five per cent of patients were men and 24pc women. In April, an outbreak of mpox, which was earlier restricted to patients with a history of foreign travel, was reported from Khairpur, claiming the lives of several newborns. The babies were under treatment in the intensive care units of two hospitals. The article notes that this increase occurs as the country approaches the festive season, when travel and family gatherings are common. news.content: Share Health Department confirms 4 more Mpox cases on: Latest 18 October 2026 15:00 Runners fill Cape Town CBD for inaugural Nelson Mandela Marathon Nelson Mandela Cape Town 18 October 2026 15:00 Police making progress in recent ANC member killings: Ramaphosa African National Congress (ANC) Cyril Ramaphosa Local Government Elections 18 October 2026 14:00 Mbalula back at work following recent collapse African National Congress (ANC) Fikile Mbalula Local Government Elections Health Department confirms 4 more Mpox cases Johannesburg Mongezi Koko 18 October 2026 | 10:00 The Western Cape recorded the most cases at 18, followed by Gauteng with three, the Eastern Cape and Free State have two cases each, while KwaZulu-Natal has one. Mpox Department of Health The backs of the hands of a patient with mpox showing a characteristic rash during his recovery phase. Picture: BSIP via AFP The Department of Health has confirmed four more Mpox cases, bringing the national total to 26 since the start of the year. The Western Cape recorded the most cases at 18, followed by Gauteng with three, the Eastern Cape and Free State have two cases each, while KwaZulu-Natal has one. ALSO READ: Mpox: South Africans urged to be vigilant Health department secures limited doses of Mpox vaccines SA’s confirmed Mpox cases rises by 4 The Department of Health said 16 of the Western Cape cases are linked to local transmission, while two involved foreign nationals visiting the country. Twenty-five of the 26 people infected are male, with ages ranging from 23 to 50. The department is urging people to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms including a rash, fever, headache, muscle aches or swollen lymph nodes. “The department urges members of the public to remain vigilant and to seek healthcare promptly if they develop symptoms such as a rash, fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes or fatigue,” said the department's spokesperson Foster Mohale .... “Individuals who have been in close contact with a confirmed or suspected Mpox case should inform healthcare workers and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. Should symptoms develop, they should avoid close contact with others and seek medical attention.” Never miss a major story. The Department of Health emphasized the need for vigilance and urged individuals to seek medical attention if symptoms such as rash, fever, or swollen lymph nodes appear. analysis.brief_en: The South African Health Department confirmed four additional Mpox cases on 18 October 2026, bringing the national total to 26 since the start of the year. The Western Cape reported the most cases (18), followed by Gauteng (3), Eastern Cape and Free State (2 each), and KwaZulu-Natal (1). Of the Western Cape cases, 16 are linked to local transmission, while two involve foreign nationals. The majority of infected individuals are male, aged 23 to 50. The department is urging the public to remain vigilant and seek medical attention if symptoms such as rash, fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, or fatigue appear. It also advised close contacts of confirmed or suspected cases to monitor themselves for 21 days and avoid close contact if symptoms develop. The response remains ongoing, with no explicit risk level stated, but the department is actively managing the situation through communication and monitoring.

Home World News Wars and Conflicts Technology UFO & Aliens Historical Mysteries Fascinating but Strange Home › World News › Monkeypox alert near Moscow: Five hospitalized after contact with suspected carrier as doctors investigate possible spread in Russia By Anastasia Prizma / 2026-10-16 / World News Monkeypox alert near Moscow: Five hospitalized Russian authorities are investigating a suspected case of monkeypox in the Moscow region after five people were hospitalized after coming into contact with a possible carrier of the virus. This has raised new concerns, as doctors conduct tests to determine whether the virus has spread. Five patients, three men and two women, have been placed under medical observation. Samples have been collected for laboratory analysis, and regional authorities have launched an epidemiological investigation. There is currently no confirmed evidence that any of the five people have been infected. Russian health authorities described their condition as satisfactory and stated that they are monitoring the situation. According to Russian media reports, the patients had contact with a person suspected of being infected with the virus. Authorities have begun identifying other possible contacts and implementing preventative measures, including disinfection. The absence of symptoms does not automatically rule out infection. Monkeypox, also known as mpox, can have an incubation period of up to 21 days. Therefore, healthcare workers monitor people exposed to the virus for signs of illness. The virus can be spread through close physical contact with an infected person, including contact with skin lesions and bodily fluids. Transmission can also occur through contaminated clothing, towels, or bedding. Prolonged face-to-face contact can be another route of infection. Symptoms can include fever, headache, muscle aches, swollen lymph nodes, and a characteristic rash. The lesions can develop into painful blisters. Many people recover within two to four weeks, although severe illness is possible, especially among vulnerable groups. The suspected case emerged after another case in Russia attracted attention. In early October, the death of a laboratory technician in Siberia prompted precautionary surveillance of people who may have been exposed to dangerous infections. Russian authorities later stated that thousands of tests revealed no signs of plague among those who had been in contact with the infected individual during this investigation. A connection between the two incidents has not yet been established. The monkeypox situation near Moscow remains under investigation. Five hospitalized individuals are under observation, awaiting laboratory test results. Their hospitalization does not necessarily mean they have tested positive. In the coming days, it should become clearer whether the suspected exposure has led to any infections. UkrMedia News Home News Economy Science and technology Politics World Lifestyle Society home World Monkeypox has reached St Petersburg: four people have been hospitalised Four cases of monkeypox have been reported in St Petersburg, Russia. A further five people in the Moscow region are under medical supervision. What is known about the infection?. World Monkeypox has reached St Petersburg: four people have been hospitalised All patients in St Petersburg were taken to Botkin Hospital. In Zhukovsky, the test results for the five hospitalised patients are still pending. by Yuriy Butusov - 16/10/2026 0 URL copy Facebook X Telegram On 16 October, Russia reported four laboratory-confirmed cases of mpox in St Petersburg. The patients have been hospitalised and their condition is assessed as moderate. In the Moscow Region, a further five people who have been in contact with a suspected carrier of the infection are under medical supervision: they are asymptomatic and are awaiting test results. Briefly about the main points Four cases of mpox have been laboratory-confirmed in St Petersburg. Hospitalised patients are being treated at the Botkin Hospital. Those who had been in contact with the patient in Zhukovsky were taken to Ramenskoye Hospital. They have no symptoms or clinical signs of the disease. Rospotrebnadzor is conducting an epidemiological investigation and has issued an order to carry out disinfection. Add UkrMedia to your Google sources Get more of our news in the recommendations. Patients in St Petersburg were taken to an infectious diseases hospital Russian media outlets REN TV, *Kommersant* and local media reported on the hospitalisation. According to SHOT, the people were taken from a residential building on Piskarevsky Prospekt in the Krasnogvardeisky district and transported to the Botkin Clinical Infectious Diseases Hospital. Read also: The Cabinet of Ministers has authorised hospitals to remain open during a «yellow» alert The Cabinet of Ministers has set out how hospitals are to operate during an emergency: at yellow alert level, admissions continue; at red alert level, patients... . According to initial reports, the patients had a high temperature and swollen lymph nodes. «Fontanka» also reported on the hospitalisation of people with monkeypox, citing its own source; however, at the time of publication, the publication was still clarifying the exact number of cases. People who have been in contact with the case in Zhukovsky are asymptomatic and are awaiting test results The individuals were admitted to hospital on 15 October following contact with a person suspected of having mpox. They are three men and two women who lived in the same flat; the probable exposure to the source of infection took place on 10 October. They are at the Ramenskaya Hospital. The chief medical officer Serhiy Markitan told Interfax that all the patients are in a satisfactory condition. Samples have been taken from them for testing, and the results are due to be provided by Russian Federal Service for Consumer Rights Protection. The health service is identifying those who have been in contact with the patient and carrying out disinfection The regional office of Rospotrebnadzor has launched a sanitary and epidemiological investigation following reports of a possible outbreak in the Moscow Region. Experts are identifying those who have been in contact with infected individuals, organising anti-epidemic measures and issuing an order for disinfection to be carried out. The department stated that the situation is under control. There is no official confirmation of a large-scale spread of mpox between regions. Find out more новини Читати новини Новини How is mpox transmitted, and when should you see a doctor? Mpox is a viral infection transmitted primarily through close physical contact with an infected person. The World Health Organisation lists a rash, fever, headache, muscle pain, swollen lymph nodes and fatigue as possible symptoms. The infection may be more dangerous for children, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems. The WHO recommends avoiding close contact with people who have characteristic symptoms, washing your hands and seeking medical advice if you suspect you have been infected. monkeypox outbreak has been suspected in the Moscow region: 5 people hospitalized Kyiv • UNN October 15 2026, 08:24 PM • 3566 views Five people were hospitalized after contact with a patient suspected of having monkeypox. They have no symptoms, and their tests are still being checked. In Russia’s Moscow Region, 5 people who had contact with a patient suspected of having monkeypox were hospitalized. Doctors are testing them for the infection, while regional authorities say they are monitoring the situation. The Moscow Times reports, according to UNN. Details The Moscow Region Ministry of Health said that all those hospitalized had undergone the necessary examinations and had samples taken. They are currently under doctors’ supervision. According to preliminary data, none of the 5 patients has symptoms of the disease. Doctors describe their condition as satisfactory. At the same time, there is currently no information confirming a new case of infection. Cases of monkeypox have already been recorded in the region In February 2026, several cases of infection were detected in the Moscow suburbs. At that time, a man suspected of having monkeypox was admitted to a hospital in Domodedovo, and the diagnosis was later confirmed. A person who had been in contact with him was hospitalized afterward. Another 2 weeks later, the disease was diagnosed in 2 tourists who had arrived in St. Petersburg from Thailand. For reference Monkeypox is a viral infection that can cause fever, enlarged lymph nodes, and painful skin rashes. The disease is most widespread in African countries. According to Russian virologist Vitaly Zverev, some species of rodents are natural carriers of the virus. People can become infected through contact with infected animals, including through bites or scratches. news.title_zh: 健康:研究发现 猴痘 幸存者需要的不仅仅是医疗治疗 - NewVision.co.ug
news.source_body_en: A recent study highlighted that Mpox survivors in Uganda need more than just medical treatment to fully recover, according to a report by NewVision.co.ug. The article, published on October 18, 2026, focuses on the health implications for those who have survived the Mpox virus. However, the evidence provided does not include specific case counts, death tolls, or detailed risk assessments related to the outbreak. The study's findings suggest a need for broader support systems for Mpox survivors beyond clinical care. The article also mentions other topics such as Uganda's Independence celebrations and economic issues, but these are not directly related to the Mpox virus. The content is based on a full original report body, and no further details on the scale of the outbreak or its impact on the population are provided.
news.content_zh: 根据 NewVision.co.ug 的一份报告,最近的一项研究强调,乌干达的 猴痘 幸存者需要的不仅仅是医疗 治疗 才能完全康复。这篇文章发表于 2026 年 10 月 18 日,重点关注 猴痘病毒 幸存者的健康影响。然而,提供的证据不包括具体病例数、死亡人数或与 暴发 相关的详细风险评估。该研究的结果表明,除了临床护理之外,猴痘 幸存者还需要更广泛的支持系统。文章还提到了其他主题,例如乌干达的独立庆祝活动和经济问题,但这些与 猴痘病毒 没有直接关系。该内容基于完整的原始报告正文,没有提供有关 暴发 的规模或其对人口影响的进一步详细信息。

news.content: Apps A A A 繁 简 Eng Menu News Homepage Latest News Video Gallery News Programmes Photo Gallery News Bulletins News Archive Send To RTHK News Error News Archive Live Video News 2026.10.19 Monday 27°C 80% Search 20252026 123456789101112 12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031 Latest News Local Greater China World News Finance Sport News Bulletins Photo Gallery Video Gallery Can search within past 12 months Home Latest News Local Mong Kok sauna patrons urged to get Mpox tests 2026-10-14 HKT 11:55 Share this story The Centre for Health Protection's Albert Au says patrons of the Hu-Tong club in Mong Kok should call a hotline where Mpox screening can be arranged for anyone with symptoms. Photo: RTHK The Centre for Health Protection is urging people who have recently visited a Mong Kok sauna to get screened for Mpox, after a patron was confirmed with the viral illness. The 39-year-old man was said to have had high-risk sexual contact with other male patrons of the Hu-Tong club. Authorities have confirmed 31 Mpox cases in Hong Kong so far this year. Speaking on an RTHK radio programme on Wednesday, the head of the centre's communicable disease branch, Albert Au, said he believed the latest infection might only be an isolated case and not an outbreak. “This patient frequented a sauna named Hu-Tong at Shanghai Street in Mong Kok multiple times during the incubation period and had high-risk sexual contact there," he said. "We believe it is highly likely that he had been infected at Hu-Tong. "Since we cannot rule out the possibility that he had been infected there, we have recommended that Hu-Tong be temporarily closed as a precaution.” While the incubation period for the virus usually lasts for six to 13 days, Au said it can be as short as a day or as long as 21 days. He noted that early symptoms are similar to other viral infections, which may include fever, chills, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes. But a rash is the most crucial symptom, Au said, eventually forming into scabs. He urged those who have been to the sauna on or after September 14 to reach out to the Mpox hotline on 2125-2373 as soon as possible to undergo a health assessment. The centre will arrange testing for those with symptoms. Au said 22 confirmed cases had been recorded since August and that the majority of them had used dating apps to look for sexual partners. He said it has been a challenge for authorities to trace all contacts, as some of the infected patients had been unable to get back in touch with their sexual partners. Photo: RTHK The Centre for Health Protection is urging people who have recently visited a Mong Kok sauna to get screened for Mpox, after a patron was confirmed with the viral illness. The 39-year-old man was said to have had high-risk sexual contact with other male patrons of the Hu-Tong club. Authorities have confirmed 31 Mpox cases in Hong Kong so far this year. Speaking on an RTHK radio programme on Wednesday, the head of the centre's communicable disease branch, Albert Au, said he believed the latest infection might only be an isolated case and not an outbreak. “This patient frequented a sauna named Hu-Tong at Shanghai Street in Mong Kok multiple times during the incubation period and had high-risk sexual contact there," he said. "We believe it is highly likely that he had been infected at Hu-Tong. "Since we cannot rule out the possibility that he had been infected there, we have recommended that Hu-Tong be temporarily closed as a precaution.” While the incubation period for the virus usually lasts for six to 13 days, Au said it can be as short as a day or as long as 21 days. He noted that early symptoms are similar to other viral infections, which may include fever, chills, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes. But a rash is the most crucial symptom, Au said, eventually forming into scabs. He urged those who have been to the sauna on or after September 14 to reach out to the Mpox hotline on 2125-2373 as soon as possible to undergo a health assessment. The centre will arrange testing for those with symptoms. Au said 22 confirmed cases had been recorded since August and that the majority of them had used dating apps to look for sexual partners. He said it has been a challenge for authorities to trace all contacts, as some of the infected patients had been unable to get back in touch with their sexual partners. analysis.location_and_population: Mong Kok, Hong Kong; patrons of the Hu-Tong club, individuals with high-risk sexual contact, and those who visited the sauna on or after September 14.
analysis.event: A 39-year-old man was confirmed with Mpox after having high-risk sexual contact at the Hu-Tong club in Mong Kok. The Centre for Health Protection is urging patrons of the club to get Mpox tests if they have symptoms.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 31 confirmed Mpox cases in Hong Kong this year, with 22 cases recorded since August. The majority of cases involved individuals using dating apps for sexual partners. The latest infection is considered an isolated case, not an outbreak.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Centre for Health Protection has recommended the temporary closure of the Hu-Tong club as a precaution. Contact tracing is ongoing, but some patients have been unable to reach out to their sexual partners. Testing is being arranged for those with symptoms.

analysis.brief_en: On October 14, 2026, the Centre for Health Protection in Hong Kong urged patrons of the Hu-Tong sauna in Mong Kok to get Mpox tests if they exhibit symptoms, following the confirmation of a 39-year-old man with the virus. The man reportedly had high-risk sexual contact with other male patrons at the club. Authorities have confirmed 31 Mpox cases in Hong Kong this year, with 22 cases since August, and the majority linked to dating app usage. The latest case is considered isolated, not an outbreak. The club was temporarily closed as a precaution, and contact tracing is ongoing, though some patients could not trace their sexual partners. Testing is being arranged for those with symptoms, and the hotline 2125-2373 is recommended for health assessments.

supplementary_news.title: Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs
supplementary_news.excerpt: A new computational study maps the host genes dysregulated in MPOX and identifies five repurposable drug candidates supported by docking and molecular dynamics simulations.

supplementary_news.content_title: Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs
supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Host Gene Study Reveals Monkeypox Mechanisms and Points to Repurposed Drugs Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram When monkeypox virus, now widely referred to as MPOX, began spreading beyond its traditional African strongholds in 2022, the world was forced to reconsider a disease long classified as a neglected tropical condition. What had once been a largely localized public health concern rapidly became a global problem, exposing glaring gaps in preparedness, therapeutics, and public awareness. Although vaccines originally developed against smallpox offer some cross-protection, most of the world’s population remains unvaccinated, whether because of limited availability, hesitancy, or simple lack of awareness. More striking still is the absence of any officially approved drug specifically targeting MPOX. A new computational study published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases by Sabkat Mahmud, Alvira Ajadee, and colleagues addresses this therapeutic vacuum by combining host transcriptomics, network biology, and molecular simulation to map the disease’s inner workings and to nominate existing drugs that might be redirected against it. The research team’s strategy rested on a deceptively simple premise: rather than studying the virus in isolation, they examined how human cells respond to infection. Viruses are obligate hijackers, and the genes a host cell switches on or off during infection often reveal the molecular levers the pathogen pulls. The investigators mined three independent transcriptomic profile datasets comparing gene expression in MPOX patients against healthy controls. By intersecting the results across datasets, they filtered out noise and arrived at 166 common host differentially expressed genes, or hDEGs, that consistently distinguish infected individuals from uninfected ones. Of these, 75 genes were upregulated, meaning their activity increased during infection, while 91 were downregulated, suggesting suppression of functions the virus may find inconvenient. Identifying differentially expressed genes is only the first step in untangling a disease process. To separate genuine drivers from incidental bystanders, the team turned to protein-protein interaction network analysis, a technique that maps the web of physical and functional contacts among the proteins encoded by the altered genes. Genes sitting at highly connected nodes of such networks often exert outsized influence on cellular behavior. From this analysis, six top-ranked host key genes emerged as potential MPOX-causing genes: ALB, HSP90AA1, CDH1, PTPRC, IGF1, and ABL1. Each tells a plausible story. ALB encodes serum albumin, the body’s most abundant plasma protein and a marker of liver function and fluid balance. HSP90AA1 is a molecular chaperone that stabilizes many client proteins, including those involved in immune signaling. CDH1 produces E-cadherin, a cell adhesion molecule critical to maintaining epithelial barriers, the very front line that poxviruses breach. PTPRC, better known as CD45, is a tyrosine phosphatase essential for lymphocyte activation, pointing to immune cell involvement. IGF1 governs growth factor signaling, and ABL1 is a kinase with well-characterized roles in cell proliferation and DNA damage responses. With these six hub genes in hand, the researchers performed functional enrichment analysis to determine which biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and signaling pathways the genes collectively implicate. Such enrichment analysis asks whether a set of genes is overrepresented in known functional categories compared with what chance would predict. The results painted a coherent picture of MPOX pathogenesis, highlighting processes tied to immune response regulation, epithelial integrity, and metabolic adaptation. The team also extended the analysis to KEGG pathways, a curated database of molecular interaction and reaction networks, which helped situate the hub genes within broader cellular circuits. Complementing this, a regulatory network analysis identified transcription factors and microRNAs that potentially control the expression of the key genes, adding another layer of mechanistic insight. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on or off, while microRNAs are small RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression after transcription; mapping these regulators helps explain how the observed expression changes might arise during infection. The second half of the study pivoted from understanding the disease to treating it. Rather than waiting years for a novel antiviral to be discovered and tested, the team pursued drug repurposing, the strategy of finding new uses for approved or well-characterized compounds. Repurposing offers a substantial speed advantage because existing drugs already have established safety profiles, manufacturing routes, and, in many cases, clinical experience in humans. The researchers screened candidate molecules against the proteins implicated in MPOX using molecular docking, a computational method that predicts how strongly and in what orientation a small molecule binds to a target protein’s binding site. From this screen, five top-ranked drug candidates emerged: Tecovirimat, Beclabuvir, Maraviroc, Raltegravir, and Brincidofovir. Several of these nominations carry intriguing logic. Tecovirimat is an antiviral originally developed against smallpox that inhibits the VP37 envelope protein of orthopoxviruses, the viral family that includes monkeypox, and it has already seen emergency use during recent outbreaks. Brincidofovir is a lipid conjugate of cidofovir designed to accumulate in cells and disrupt viral DNA replication, and it too carries orthopoxvirus indications. Maraviroc, by contrast, is an HIV entry inhibitor that blocks the CCR5 receptor on immune cells, while Raltegravir is an HIV integrase strand transfer inhibitor, and Beclabuvir is an investigational hepatitis C NS5A inhibitor. That compounds developed for entirely different pathogens dock favorably onto host or viral proteins relevant to MPOX illustrates the core promise of repurposing: molecular interfaces evolved for one purpose can sometimes be exploited for another. Computational docking alone can be misleading, however, because a molecule that fits a binding site in a static snapshot may fail to maintain that interaction under the dynamic conditions of a living cell. To address this, the team evaluated the pharmacokinetic credentials of all five candidates using ADME/T analysis, which assesses absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, alongside drug-likeness filters that compare molecular properties against those of successful oral medicines. The candidates passed these evaluations with favorable profiles, suggesting that, in principle, they could reach their targets in the body at effective concentrations without unacceptable toxicity. The strongest computational evidence came from molecular dynamics simulations, which model the physical motion of atoms over time to test whether a drug-protein complex remains stable in a realistic, fluctuating environment. The researchers ran 100-nanosecond simulations of the three most promising complexes: ALB bound to Tecovirimat, CDH1 bound to Maraviroc, and PPARG bound to Beclabuvir. PPARG, the nuclear receptor targeted by Beclabuvir in this analysis, adds an interesting metabolic dimension to the proposed mechanism. Throughout the simulations, the team tracked root-mean-square deviation, or RMSD, which measures how far the protein structure drifts from its starting conformation, and root-mean-square fluctuation, or RMSF, which quantifies how much individual residues wiggle locally. They also computed binding free energies using the MM-GBSA method, which estimates the thermodynamic favorability of the drug-protein interaction. All three complexes demonstrated strong binding stability across these metrics, indicating that the docked poses were not artifacts of a single frozen structure but held up under sustained atomic motion. The convergence of transcriptomic evidence, network analysis, docking, pharmacokinetic screening, and dynamic simulation gives the study an unusually complete computational arc, moving from disease mechanism to therapeutic nomination within a single framework. The identification of host key genes such as ALB, CDH1, and PTPRC may also inform diagnostic development, since consistently dysregulated host transcripts can serve as biomarkers distinguishing MPOX from other febrile illnesses, a persistent challenge in regions where poxvirus, malaria, and other infections overlap clinically. Yet the authors are careful to frame their findings as a starting point rather than a conclusion. Every result in the study, from the 166 differentially expressed genes to the stability of the simulated drug complexes, derives from computational inference and must be validated experimentally in the laboratory before it can inform clinical practice. Docking scores do not guarantee efficacy in infected cells, and transcriptomic correlations do not prove causation. Still, in a landscape where no approved MPOX drug exists and vaccine coverage remains sparse, computational pipelines like this one offer a rapid, systematic way to prioritize which existing molecules deserve the first laboratory look. As MPOX continues to circulate globally, such approaches may shorten the path from genomic data to actionable therapeutics, turning the growing archive of patient transcriptomes into a roadmap for fighting a disease the world can no longer afford to neglect.
